\subsubsection{Multiple variables}\label{multiple-variables}

What if you want to obtain all results summarised by multiple groupings? Let's obtain the results grouped by the levels of \texttt{AgeSubject}, \texttt{WordCategory} and \texttt{Voice} and we want to save the output.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, WordCategory, Voice) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{count =} \FunctionTok{n}\NormalTok{(),}
            \AttributeTok{range\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{range}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
            \AttributeTok{mean\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
            \AttributeTok{sd\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{sd}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
            \AttributeTok{var\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{var}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
            \AttributeTok{min\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{min}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
            \AttributeTok{max\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{max}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
            \AttributeTok{quart1\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{quantile}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{),}
            \AttributeTok{quart1\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{quantile}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec, }\FloatTok{0.75}\NormalTok{),}
            \AttributeTok{median\_RTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{median}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec)) }\OtherTok{{-}\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{ dfMeans}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}

\subsection{Summary tables}\label{summary-tables}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Using \texttt{summarytools}}{Using summarytools}}\label{using-summarytools}

Using the package \texttt{summarytools} you can obtain nice table ready for publications!

\paragraph{Summary of full dataset with graphs}\label{summary-of-full-dataset-with-graphs}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{dfSummary}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{graph.col =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{style =} \StringTok{"grid"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{stview}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"render"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{Descriptive statistics for numeric variables}\label{descriptive-statistics-for-numeric-variables}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{descr}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{stview}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"render"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Non-numerical variable(s) ignored: Word, AgeSubject, WordCategory, CV, Obstruent, Frication, Voice
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{Frequencies for non-numeric variables}\label{frequencies-for-non-numeric-variables}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{freq}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{stview}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"render"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Variable(s) ignored: RTlexdec, RTnaming, Familiarity, WrittenFrequency, WrittenSpokenFrequencyRatio, FamilySize, DerivationalEntropy, InflectionalEntropy, NumberSimplexSynsets, NumberComplexSynsets, MeanBigramFrequency, FrequencyInitialDiphone, ConspelV, ConspelN, ConphonV, ConphonN, ConfriendsV, ConfriendsN, ConffN, ConfbV, ConfbN, NounFrequency, VerbFrequency
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Using \texttt{gtsummary}}{Using gtsummary}}\label{using-gtsummary}

We use the \texttt{gtsummary} package to create nice tables for publication. This package is very useful for creating publication ready tables with descriptive statistics, regression models, etc. See \href{https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/index.html}{this link} for more details on the various options possible with this package.

\paragraph{Basic summaries}\label{basic-summaries-1}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}  
  \FunctionTok{tbl\_summary}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{include =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, RTlexdec, Familiarity, WordCategory, Voice))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{table}[t]

\paragraph{With statistics (comparing means)}\label{with-statistics-comparing-means}

We use the two \texttt{numeric\ outcomes} and assess differences between the two groups.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}  
  \FunctionTok{tbl\_summary}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{include =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec, RTnaming),}
              \AttributeTok{by =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\CommentTok{\# split table by AgeSubject}
              \AttributeTok{missing =} \StringTok{"no"} \CommentTok{\# don\textquotesingle{}t list missing data separately}
\NormalTok{  ) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}  
  \FunctionTok{add\_n}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}  \CommentTok{\# add column with total number of non{-}missing observations}
  \FunctionTok{add\_p}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}  \CommentTok{\# test for a difference between groups}
  \FunctionTok{modify\_header}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{label =} \StringTok{"**Variable**"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}  \CommentTok{\# update the column header}
  \FunctionTok{bold\_labels}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{table}[t]
\fontsize{12.0pt}{14.0pt}\selectfont

\midrule\addlinespace[2.5pt]
{\bfseries RTlexdec} & 4,568 & 6.64 (6.57, 6.73) & 6.43 (6.36, 6.51) & <0.001 \\ 
{\bfseries RTnaming} & 4,568 & 6.49 (6.45, 6.53) & 6.15 (6.12, 6.18) & <0.001 \\

\end{tabular*}

\textsuperscript{\textit{2}}Wilcoxon rank sum test\\
\end{minipage}
\end{table}

\subsection{Visualisation}\label{visualisation}

In the \texttt{tidyverse}, the package for making elegant plots is called \texttt{ggplot2}. It works a lot like how pipes work, but since it was originally designed as a separate package, it uses \texttt{+} instead of \texttt{\%\textgreater{}\%}.

\subsubsection{First steps}\label{first-steps-1}

\paragraph{Empty plot area}\label{empty-plot-area}

Let's produce a basic plot with nothing drawn on it.
This is the basic plotting area in \texttt{R}. We need to then add layers on top of it to show our plot

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-92-1.pdf}}

\paragraph{Adding x and y values}\label{adding-x-and-y-values}

Let's add the x and y values from our dataset. X = subjective familiarity rating, y = RT in Visual Lexical Decision task

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ Familiarity, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-93-1.pdf}}

There are no differences between the two. We need to tell \texttt{ggplot2} to add a geometric function for plotting

\paragraph{Adding geoms}\label{adding-geoms}

Geoms are integrated within \texttt{ggplot2} to obtain various types of plots.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ Familiarity, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-94-1.pdf}}

\paragraph{Adding line of best fit}\label{adding-line-of-best-fit}

We will add a line of best fit. This is used to evaluate presence/absence of a relationship between two numeric variables

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ Familiarity, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_smooth}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"lm"}\NormalTok{) }\DocumentationTok{\#\# line of best fit based on the lm() method}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
\end{verbatim}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-95-1.pdf}}

The result shows a nice negative correlation! RT lexical decision decreases when familiarity rating increases.

We can ask, are there differences related to the word category, i.e., verb vs noun?

\paragraph{By word category}\label{by-word-category}

We change colour by levels of word category;

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ Familiarity, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec,}
             \AttributeTok{colour =}\NormalTok{ WordCategory)) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DocumentationTok{\#\# add colour to the base aesthetics}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_smooth}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"lm"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
\end{verbatim}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-96-1.pdf}}

\paragraph{Making final touches}\label{making-final-touches}

Let's add a title and a subtitle, change x and y labels, change size of overall plot, and colours of the categories.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ Familiarity, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec,}
             \AttributeTok{colour =}\NormalTok{ WordCategory)) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DocumentationTok{\#\# add colour to the base aesthetics}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_smooth}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"lm"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{labs}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =} \StringTok{"Familiarity rating"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{y =} \StringTok{"RT Lexical Decision"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{title =} \StringTok{"Familiarity rating vs RT in a lexical decision task"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{subtitle =} \StringTok{"with a trend line"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DocumentationTok{\#\# add labels}
  \FunctionTok{theme}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{text =} \FunctionTok{element\_text}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{size =} \DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DocumentationTok{\#\# increase size of plot}
  \FunctionTok{theme}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{legend.position =} \StringTok{"bottom"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{legend.title =} \FunctionTok{element\_blank}\NormalTok{()) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DocumentationTok{\#\# remove legend title and change position}
  \FunctionTok{scale\_color\_manual}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Nouns"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Verbs"}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{values =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"blue"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"red"}\NormalTok{)) }\DocumentationTok{\#\# change colours and names of legend}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
\end{verbatim}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-97-1.pdf}}

To choose colours, use the addin \texttt{colourpicker} from above. See this \href{http://applied-r.com/r-color-tables/}{link} for full list of colours available. Use colours that are colour-blind friendly \href{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/colorBlindness/vignettes/colorBlindness.html}{here}

\subsubsection{Additional plots}\label{additional-plots}

We looked above at one example of plots (with points). We could use additional types of plots.

\paragraph{A bar plot}\label{a-bar-plot}

Will show barplots of the dataset

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec, }
             \AttributeTok{colour =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_bar}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-98-1.pdf}}

And another view with error bars! This is a nice example that shows how you can combine multiple chains with the pipe:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Group by Age of subject
\item
  Compute mean and SD
\item
  use ggplot2 syntax to plot a barplot and error bars
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}
    \AttributeTok{sd =} \FunctionTok{sd}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
    \AttributeTok{RTlexdecM =} \FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec)}
\NormalTok{  ) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdecM)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_col}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{fill =} \StringTok{"lightgray"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{color =} \StringTok{"black"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_errorbar}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{ymin =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdecM}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{sd, }\AttributeTok{ymax =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdecM}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{sd), }\AttributeTok{width =} \FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-99-1.pdf}}

\subsubsection{Advanced plots}\label{advanced-plots}

We will use the package \texttt{ggdist} \href{https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/}{see here}which allows us to obtain various plots adding the distributions.

\paragraph{A dotplot}\label{a-dotplot}

This dotplot allow to display the distribution of the dataframe showing their density

\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}

\paragraph{Rain cloud plots}\label{rain-cloud-plots}

Rain clouds are used to combine both a density plot with dotplots in the same figure. These can be informative as to the overall distribution of the dataset.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec,}
             \AttributeTok{fill =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{stat\_slab}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{thickness =} \FunctionTok{after\_stat}\NormalTok{(pdf}\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{n)), }\AttributeTok{scale =} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{stat\_dotsinterval}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{side =} \StringTok{"bottom"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{scale =} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{slab\_linewidth =} \ConstantTok{NA}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{scale\_fill\_brewer}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{palette =} \StringTok{"Set2"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-106-1.pdf}}

\paragraph{Eye plots and half-eye plots}\label{eye-plots-and-half-eye-plots}

We can also obtain density plots with eye plots and half-eye plots. These are similar to rain clouds but allow you to see the distribution of the data in a different way. For these plots, using \texttt{stat\_slabinterval()} with \texttt{side\ =\ "both",\ "top",\ "bottom",\ "right",\ or\ "left"} you can adjust positions of the eye plots. Note that with \texttt{"top",\ or\ "bottom"}, the \texttt{y} value is a categorical predictor and the \texttt{x} is a numeric outcome.

\subparagraph{Eye plot}\label{eye-plot}

We can use \texttt{stat\_eye()} or \texttt{stat\_slabinterval(side\ =\ "both")} to obtain eye plots.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec,}
             \AttributeTok{fill =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{stat\_eye}\NormalTok{() }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-107-1.pdf}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec,}
             \AttributeTok{fill =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{stat\_slabinterval}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{side =} \StringTok{"both"}\NormalTok{) }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-107-2.pdf}}

We can use \texttt{stat\_halfeye()} or \texttt{stat\_slabinterval()} to obtain half-eye plots. Use \texttt{stat\_slabinterval(side\ =\ "left")} or \texttt{stat\_slabinterval(side\ =\ "right")} to obtain half-eye plots on the left or right side of the plot, respectively.

\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}

\end{Highlighting}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-108-1.pdf}}

\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec,}
             \AttributeTok{fill =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}

\subsubsection{Facet\_grid}\label{facet_grid}

The plots we used so far allowed to plot data as a function of one categorical variable, e.g., \texttt{AgeSubject}. What if we wanted to show the different patterns emerging when combining \texttt{AgeSubject} (old vs young), \texttt{WordCategory} (Noun or Verb), \texttt{CV} (Consonant or Vowel) and \texttt{Voice} (Voiced and Voiceless) ?
What if we also wanted to modify the labels and order of levels of variables?

We will start slowly below to show how we can combine two categorical variables and extend them to additional ones

\paragraph{Two categorical variables}\label{two-categorical-variables}

\subparagraph{First steps}\label{first-steps-2}

Here we obtain a boxplot with two categorical variables \texttt{AgeSubject} and \texttt{WordCategory}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{facet\_grid}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ WordCategory)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-109-1.pdf}}

\subparagraph{Changing order of levels within a variable and its labels}\label{changing-order-of-levels-within-a-variable-and-its-labels}

What would you do to change both order of levels within a variable and its labels? We want to change order for \texttt{AgeSubject} to be Young vs Old (rather than old vs young) and change labels of \texttt{WordCategory} from N vs V to Noun vs Verb?

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeSubject =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Old"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{WordCategory =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Noun"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Verb"}\NormalTok{))) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{facet\_grid}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ WordCategory)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-110-1.pdf}}

\paragraph{Three or more categorical variables}\label{three-or-more-categorical-variables}

Let us obtain a boxplot with four categorical variables \texttt{AgeSubject}, \texttt{WordCategory}, \texttt{CV} and \texttt{Voice}. We still need to change names.
We can also add \texttt{margins\ =\ TRUE} to obtain mean values for all categories (under \texttt{all}). We can also use \texttt{scale\ =\ "free"} to change limits of the \texttt{y-axis}.

Of course this figure is so complex that it needs a lot of interpretation. But it allows you to see how we can use \texttt{facet\_grid} to get more categorical variables in. This visualisation suggests that there are no clear differences when plotting results by this 4-way interaction as we always have clear differences between ``Young'' and ``Old'' participants, with ``Young'' being faster than ``Old'' participants.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeSubject =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Old"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{WordCategory =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Noun"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Verb"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{CV =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(CV, }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Consonant"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Vowel"}\NormalTok{))) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{facet\_grid}\NormalTok{(CV }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ Voice }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{margins =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{scales =} \StringTok{"free"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-111-1.pdf}}

\paragraph{Comparing two numeric outcomes}\label{comparing-two-numeric-outcomes}

What if we want to compare performance in relation to reaction time for the lexical decision task (RTlexdec) and reaction time for naming (RTnaming). We want to see if there are differences related to the \texttt{AgeSubject}, \texttt{WordCategory}.
We use \texttt{pivot\_longer} here to do change the format of our table and then change names and use \texttt{facet\_grid}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec, RTnaming, AgeSubject, WordCategory) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{pivot\_longer}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{cols =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec, RTnaming),}
               \AttributeTok{names\_to =} \StringTok{"variable"}\NormalTok{,}
               \AttributeTok{values\_to =} \StringTok{"values"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeSubject =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Old"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{WordCategory =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Noun"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Verb"}\NormalTok{))) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ variable, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ values)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{facet\_grid}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{margins =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{scales =} \StringTok{"free"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-112-1.pdf}}

\paragraph{Exporting images}\label{exporting-images}

When you use Rmarkdown, your figures are already embedded within the generated output. If you are using an R script and/or want to add the figure in a different document, you can use the following code:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{jpeg}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{filename =} \FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"outputs/test.jpeg"}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{width =} \DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{height =} \DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{units =} \StringTok{"cm"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{res =} \DecValTok{300}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec, RTnaming, AgeSubject, WordCategory) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{pivot\_longer}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{cols =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec, RTnaming),}
               \AttributeTok{names\_to =} \StringTok{"variable"}\NormalTok{,}
               \AttributeTok{values\_to =} \StringTok{"values"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeSubject =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Old"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{WordCategory =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Noun"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Verb"}\NormalTok{))) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ variable, }
             \AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ values)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{facet\_grid}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{margins =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{scales =} \StringTok{"free"}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{dev.off}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## pdf 
##   2
\end{verbatim}

The image is automatically saved into your working directory and you can import it to your word (\LaTeX) document.

You can use any device to save the output. Jpeg, PNG, PDF, TIFF, etc..
From an R script, you can run the code and then the image will appear within the ``Plots'' area. Simply click on export and you will be able to save the image.

\subsubsection{Conclusion}\label{conclusion}

As you can see, visualisations in \texttt{R} using the \texttt{Tidyverse} provide you with many options and you can explore these further.

See \href{https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/}{here} for a full list of geoms. This will help you in thinking about visualisation.

See extensions to ggplot2 \href{https://exts.ggplot2.tidyverse.org/gallery/}{here} for additional plugins to enhance plots.

\section{PhonR}\label{phonr}

\subsection{Intro}\label{intro}

These two packages allow to do various things with phoneticy data. \href{https://drammock.github.io/phonR/}{PhonR} former allows to normalise data and generate nice plots; the Vowels is a suite of normalisation procedures and plotting functions (it used to be an online platform, but this is not working anymore! \href{http://lvc.uoregon.edu/norm/}{see here} or \href{http://ncslaap.lib.ncsu.edu/tools/norm/}{here}). See help for \href{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/vowels/vowels.pdf}{Vowels}.

We'll heavily use PhonR as it provides standard and many advanced options for normalisation and plotting, etc..

I am borrowing many examples from the \href{https://drammock.github.io/phonR/}{PhonR} link. You can adapt the codes below to your own data

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\subsection{Calculating vowel space area}\label{calculating-vowel-space-area}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{poly.area }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{with}\NormalTok{(indo, }\FunctionTok{vowelMeansPolygonArea}\NormalTok{(f1, f2, vowel, }\AttributeTok{poly.order =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"i"}\NormalTok{, }
    \StringTok{"e"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"a"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"o"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"u"}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{group =}\NormalTok{ subj))}
\NormalTok{hull.area }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{with}\NormalTok{(indo, }\FunctionTok{convexHullArea}\NormalTok{(f1, f2, }\AttributeTok{group =}\NormalTok{ subj))}
\FunctionTok{rbind}\NormalTok{(poly.area, hull.area)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\part{Statistical analyses using R}\label{part-statistical-analyses-using-r}

\chapter{Correlation, LM, GLM, STD and CLM}\label{Corr-LM-GLM-STD-CLM}

This chapter introduces you to the basics of inferential statistics. We
cover correlation tests to identify specific patterns in the data. We
then use linear models to evaluate group differences, and generalised
linear models to evaluate binary outcomes. We also introduce the basics
of signal detection theory (SDT) to evaluate the accuracy of our models.
At the end of this chapter, we introduce the basics of cumulative link
models (CLM) to evaluate ordinal (likert) outcomes on two datasets.

\section{Loading packages}\label{loading-packages-1}

\begin{Shaded}

\section{Inferential statistics}\label{inferential-statistics}

\subsection{Introduction}\label{introduction-2}

What do we mean by inferential statistics?

We want to evaluate if there are differences observed between two groups
of datapoints and if these differences are statistically significant.

For this, we need to pay attention to the format of our outcome and
predictors. An outcome is the response variable (or dependent variable);
a predictor is our independent variable(s). This is fed into our
equation

\(y = x\beta + \varepsilon\)

where:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(y\) \(\rightarrow\) outcome (DV) \(\Rightarrow\) known
\item
  \(x\) \(\rightarrow\) fixed effect (IV) \(\Rightarrow\) known
\item
  \(\beta\) \(\rightarrow\) coefficient of fixed effect \(\Rightarrow\)
  unknown
\item
  \(\varepsilon\) \(\rightarrow\) random error term \(\Rightarrow\) unknown
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Hypothesis testing}\label{hypothesis-testing}

In the approach that this book follows, we use a frequentist approach to
hypothesis testing. By frequentist we mean when modelling the
relationship between an outcome and a predictor, we are interested in
testing if the predictor has a clear and statistically significant
influence on the outcome. When evaluating this, we try to reject the
null hypothesis (\emph{H}\(_0\)) in favour of the alternative hypothesis
(\emph{H}\(_1\)).

The null hypothesis (\emph{H}\(_0\)) is the hypothesis we make that there is no
statistical evidence in favour of an effect nor of a difference between
the groups. The alternative hypothesis (\emph{H}\(_1\)) is the hypothesis we
make to reject the null hypothesis and there is indeed a statistical
evidence in favour of an effect or a difference between the groups.

\subsection{Type of outcomes}\label{type-of-outcomes}

It is important to know the class of the outcome before doing any
pre-data analyses or inferential statistics. Outcome classes can be one
of:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \texttt{Numeric}: As an example, we have length/width of leaf; height of
  mountain; fundamental frequency of the voice; etc. These are
  generally modelled with a \texttt{Gaussian} distribution These are \texttt{true}
  numbers and we can use summaries, t-tests, linear models, etc.
  Integers are a family of numeric variables and can still be
  considered as a normal numeric variable. Count data are numbers
  related to a category. In general, these are related to the second
  type of outcomes, and should be analysed using a poisson logistic
  regression
\item
  \texttt{Categorical} (Unordered): Observations for two or more categories.
  As an example, we can have gender of a speaker (male or female);
  responses to a True vs False perception tests; Colour (unordered)
  categorisation, e.g., red, blue, yellow, orange, etc.. For these we
  can use a Generalised Linear Model (binomial or multinomial) or a
  simple chi-square test.
\item
  \texttt{Categorical} (Ordered): When you run a rating experiment, where the
  outcome is either \texttt{numeric} (i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) or \texttt{categories}
  (i.e., disagree, neutral, agree). The \texttt{numeric} option is NOT a true
  number as for the participant, these are categories. Cumulative
  Logit models (or Generalised Linear Model with a cumulative
  function) are used. The mean is meaningless here, and the median is
  a preferred descriptive statistic.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Types of Errors?}\label{errors}

In the literature, we discuss various types of errors in statistical
models. There are four different types, and the excellent Sonderegger
(2023) book (Sonderegger, M. (2023). \emph{Regression Modeling for Linguistic
Data}. The MIT Press.) summarises these nicely. Here are the four types:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Type I} (or ``false positive'' or error \(\alpha\)) \(\Rightarrow\)
  falsely concluding there is an effect when none exists. (generally
  due to inaccurate modelling strategies)
\item
  \textbf{Type II} (or ``false negative'' or error \(\beta\))) \(\Rightarrow\)
  falsely concluding there is no effect when one in fact exists
  (generally due to inaccurate modelling strategies)
\end{enumerate}

\includegraphics[width=7.02083in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/type_I_II_errors.png}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item
  \textbf{Type S} \(\Rightarrow\) Inaccurate sign (generally due to \emph{hidden}
  multicollinearity and low power = 1- \(\beta\))
\item
  \textbf{Type M} \(\Rightarrow\) Inaccurate magnitude (generally due to
  \emph{hidden} multicollinearity and low power = 1- \(\beta\))
\end{enumerate}

It is important to note that the \textbf{Type I} and \textbf{Type II} errors are
the most commonly discussed in the literature and are related to each
other. Modelling is an art, and depending on model specifications, we
can easily increase \textbf{Type I} and/or \textbf{Type II} errors. \textbf{Type I} is
usually increased in the case of using inaccurately specified model,
e.g., not using a random effects structure when the data comes from
multiple speakers and/or multiple items. \textbf{Type II} error is usually
increased when there is an over specification of the model and/or not
accounting for dependencies in the data. \textbf{Type S} and \textbf{Type M} are
generally caused due to collinearity in the data, which causes
instability in the model and leads to cases of suppression; a point
discussed in \textbf{chapter} \ref{DT-RF}.

\section{Effect size and power analysis}\label{effect-size-and-power-analysis}

\subsection{Effect size}\label{effect-size}

\subsubsection{What is the purpose of Effect Size?}\label{what-is-the-purpose-of-effect-size}

`Effect size' is simply a way of quantifying the size of the difference
between two groups.

There are two family groups of Effect Size:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Standardised mean differences (also called group difference indices;
  e.g., Cohen's \emph{d}), The mean difference Effect Sizes are computed
  when the focus of the statistical analysis uses mean outcome scores
  to compare potential group differences.
\item
  Strength of association (also referred to as relationship
  variance-accounted-for or variance explained Effect Sizes; e.g.,
  \(R^{2}\), \(\eta^{2}\), \(\eta^{2}p\), \(\omega^{2}\), etc. Strength of
  association Effect Size indices are calculated across a wide variety
  of research designs (e.g., ex post facto or causal comparative,
  experimental, quasi-experimental, prediction {[}regression and
  correlational{]}) using the general linear model (GLM) for the
  statistical analyses. Strength of association Effect Sizes indicate
  how much of the variance associated with the dependent variable
  (e.g., students' English test scores) can be accounted for (or
  explained) by the independent variable(s) (e.g., gender).
\end{enumerate}

Both Effect Size families can be further categorised into biased
(uncorrected) and unbiased (corrected) measures:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Biased measures relates to \textbf{``sampling error''} and how the Effect
  Size derived from statistical procedures computed with smaller
  groups of participants (samples) drawn from a larger population will
  be higher than would be found either in the original population or
  in participant samples studied at a later date.
\end{itemize}

For example, assume a school counselling researcher randomly selects a
sample of 15 girls and 15 boys from a 10th-grade physical education
class in one high school. This 30-person sample then is assumed to
represent the entire population of male and female students attending
all Grade 10 physical education classes across a district's five high
schools. Because there is always sampling error (i.e., problems with
selecting the students to participate in the research study),
uncorrected Effect Sizes (e.g., Cohen's \emph{d}, \(R^{2}\), \(\eta^{2}\)) will
be higher (i.e., positively biased or overestimated) for the 30 students
than if the researcher actually could have included in the study every
10th-grade physical education student across all five high schools.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Unbiased ones (e.g., adjusted \(R^{2}\), Hays' \(\omega^{2}\), etc. )
  statistically correct for this positive bias by calculating the
  strength of association indices so that they better reflect the true
  Effect Sizes for the entire population and those calculated in
  future samples.
\end{itemize}

The issue is that because these formulas must adjust for sampling error
occurring both in the present study and in subsequent investigations,
Effect Size estimates for future research samples result in more
shrinkage (i.e., are smaller or more conservative) than those Effect
Size estimates based on an entire population. Therefore, interpretation
of Effect Size s is often less than straightforward and must be
exercised with caution.

\subsubsection{What is the relationship between Effect Size and Significance?}\label{what-is-the-relationship-between-effect-size-and-significance}

Effect size quantifies the size of the difference between two groups,
and may therefore be said to be a true measure of the significance of
the difference.

The statistical significance is usually calculated as a `p-value', the
probability that a difference of at least the same size would have
arisen by chance, even if there really were no difference between the
two populations. For differences between the means of two groups, this
p-value would normally be calculated from a `t-test'. By convention, if
p \textless{} 0.05 (i.e.~below 5\%), the difference is taken to be large enough to
be `significant'; if not, then it is `not significant'.

There are a number of problems with using `significance tests' in this
way. The main one is that the p-value depends essentially on two things:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  The size of the effect
\item
  The size of the sample.
\end{enumerate}

One would get a `significant' result either if the effect were very big
(despite having only a small sample) or if the sample were very big
(even if the actual effect size were tiny). It is important to know the
statistical significance of a result, since without it there is a danger
of drawing firm conclusions from studies where the sample is too small
to justify such confidence. However, statistical significance does not
tell you the most important thing: \textbf{the size of the effect}. One way
to overcome this confusion is to report the effect size, together with
an estimate of its likely `margin for error' or `confidence interval'.

\subsubsection{What is Confidence Interval?}\label{what-is-confidence-interval}

The confidence interval is an alternative way to indicate the
variability in estimates from small samples. The default calculation
here is a `95\% confidence interval'. If multiple samples of two groups
of the same size as these, taken from a population in which the true
difference was the value in column J, there would be variation in the
differences found. However, for every 100 samples taken, for 95 of them
(on average) the difference would be between the lower and upper
confidence limits. The confidence interval is usually interpreted as a
`margin of uncertainty' around the estimate of the difference between
experimental and control groups.

\subsubsection{Which Effect Size measure to use?}\label{which-effect-size-measure-to-use}

We highlighted above various effect size measures, e.g., Cohen's \emph{d},
\(R^{2}\), \(\eta^{2}\), \(\eta^{2}p\), \(\omega^{2}\). Which one to chose from?
Well, all depends on the statistical approach you are using and whether
you want to report on standardised or unstandardised measures.

However, as a rule of thumb, you can do the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  In general, if we want to talk about the sample we have, we can use
  any biased method (like the eta-squared) because it estimates only
  for the sample and not the population.
\item
  If we want to generalise our results, we have to use an unbiased
  method.
\end{enumerate}

Literature recommends using an Effect Size measure accompanied with the
Confidence Interval, because telling only that a result is statistically
significant doesn't inform us of the contribution of the independent
variable to explain the variation in the dependent variable.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{How to compute these in \texttt{R}}{How to compute these in R}}\label{how-to-compute-these-in-r}

We use the package \texttt{effectsize}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{Standardised effect sizes (Cohen's \emph{d})}{Standardised effect sizes (Cohen's d)}}\label{standardised-effect-sizes-cohens-d}

It can be computed using the following formula:

\(d=\frac{{Mean}_{factor1}-\ {Mean}_{factor2}}{{SD}_{pooled}}\)

With the pooled standard deviation computed as:

\({SD}_{pooled}=\sqrt{\frac{{SD}_{factor1}^2\ast\left({Number}_{factor1}-1\right)+\ {SD}_{factor2}^2\ast\left({Number}_{factor2}-1\right)}{{Number}_{factor1}+\ {Number}_{factor2}-\ 2}}\)

Fortunately, instead of calculating it manually, we can use the function
\texttt{cohens\_d()} from the package \texttt{effectsize}.

\subparagraph{Linear model}\label{linear-model}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{options}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{es.use\_symbols =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}\CommentTok{\# get nice symbols when printing! (On Windows, requires R \textgreater{}= 4.2.0)}

\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)      6.660958   0.002324 2866.44   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubjectyoung -0.221721   0.003286  -67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

What the model above tells us is that there is a very highly
statistically significant impact of AgeSubject on RTlexdec (p \textless{}
0.0001).

\subparagraph{\texorpdfstring{Cohen's \emph{d}}{Cohen's d}}\label{cohens-d}

However, it does not tell us how large this effect is. That is where we
can use the \texttt{cohens\_d()} function.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Cohen\textquotesingle{}s d}
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{cohens\_d}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{interpret\_cohens\_d}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Cohen's d |       95% CI | Interpretation
## -----------------------------------------
## 2.00      | [1.93, 2.07] |          large
## 
## - Estimated using pooled SD.
## - Interpretation rule: cohen1988
\end{verbatim}

One nice option in the package \texttt{effectsize} is to use an \href{https://easystats.github.io/effectsize/articles/interpret.html}{\emph{Automated
Interpretation of Indices of Effect Size}
vignette}.
We can use the original publication to interpret the effect size or use
an alternative. See the link above for more details.

We can also standardise our model's coefficients, which allows us to
compare the effect sizes of different predictors in the same model and
between models, variables and studies.

\subparagraph{Standardised coefficients}\label{standardised-coefficients}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{model }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}

\NormalTok{datawizard}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{standardize}\NormalTok{(model)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = data_std)
## 
## Coefficients:
##     (Intercept)  AgeSubjectyoung  
##          0.7065          -1.4130
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{parameters}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{standardize\_parameters}\NormalTok{(model)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # Standardization method: refit
## 
## Parameter          | Std. Coef. |         95% CI
## ------------------------------------------------
## (Intercept)        |       0.71 | [ 0.68,  0.74]
## AgeSubject [young] |      -1.41 | [-1.45, -1.37]
\end{verbatim}

Standardised coefficients are interpreted as the change in standard
deviations of the outcome variable for a one standard deviation change
in the predictor variable. We can initially standardise our outcomes
using the function \texttt{scale(center\ =\ TRUE,\ scale\ =\ TRUE)} and then run our
model, OR use the function \texttt{standardize()} from the package \texttt{datawizard}
or \texttt{standardize\_parameters()} from the package \texttt{parameters} to do that.

\paragraph{Strength of association effect sizes}\label{strength-of-association-effect-sizes}

Here, we saw already that there are biased and unbiased measures. We
will document the classical measures used.

\subparagraph{\texorpdfstring{\(R^{2}\)}{R\^{}\{2\}}}\label{r2}

\(R^{2}\) (R squared): It is the proportion of variance explained by the
model. This is a biased effect size measure. It is computed as:

\(R^2=\frac{SS_{model}}{SS_{total}}=1-\frac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}}\)

Where:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(SS_{model}\) is the sum of squares of the model
\item
  \(SS_{total}\) is the total sum of squares
\item
  \(SS_{residual}\) is the sum of squares of the residuals.
\end{itemize}

We can get the \(R^{2}\) and the adjusted \(R^{2}\) from the summary of the
model:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{r.squared}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.49923
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{adj.r.squared}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.4991203
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{\texorpdfstring{\(\eta^{2}\) (eta squared)}{\textbackslash eta\^{}\{2\} (eta squared)}}\label{eta2-eta-squared}

The eta-squared effect size measure is a biased measure and describes
the ratio of variance explained in the dependent variable by a predictor
(or factor) while controlling for other predictors (or in a simple way:
it is the proportion of total variation attributable to the factor). The
range is from 0 to 1 and it sums up to 1. Eta squared is a biased
estimator of the variance explained by the model in the population (it
only estimates effect size in the sample). On average it overestimates
the variance explained in the population. . It is computed as:

\(\eta^{2}=\frac{SS_{model}}{SS_{total}}\)

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(SS_{model}\) is the sum of squares of the model
\item
  \(SS_{total}\) is the total sum of squares
\item
  \(SS_{residual}\) is the sum of squares of the residuals.
\end{itemize}

In a sense, both \(R^{2}\) and \(\eta^{2}\) are computed in the same way.

To obtain it directly from the model, we can use the function
\texttt{eta\_squared()} from the package \texttt{effectsize} and specify
\texttt{partial\ =\ FALSE}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# eta squared}
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{aov}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{eta\_squared}\NormalTok{(., }\AttributeTok{partial =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{interpret\_eta\_squared}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)
## 
## Parameter  |   η² |       95% CI | Interpretation
## -------------------------------------------------
## AgeSubject | 0.50 | [0.48, 1.00] |          large
## 
## - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
## - Interpretation rule: field2013
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{\texorpdfstring{\(\eta^{2}p\) (partial eta squared)}{\textbackslash eta\^{}\{2\}p (partial eta squared)}}\label{eta2p-partial-eta-squared}

\(\eta^{2}p\) (partial eta squared): ``proportion of total variation
attributable to the factor, partialling out (excluding) other factors
from the total non error variation''. Partial eta squared is normally
higher than eta squared (except in simple one-factor models). The range
is from 0 to 1, and it sums up to more than 1 (except in one-way ANOVA).
It is computed as:

\(\eta^{2}p=\frac{SS_{factor}}{SS_{factor}+SS_{error}}\)

Where:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(SS_{factor}\) is the sum of squares of the factor
\item
  \(SS_{error}\) is the sum of squares of the error.
\end{itemize}

To obtain it directly from the model, we can use the function
\texttt{eta\_squared()} from the package \texttt{effectsize} and specify
\texttt{partial\ =\ TRUE}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# partial eta squared}
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{aov}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{eta\_squared}\NormalTok{(., }\AttributeTok{partial =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{interpret\_eta\_squared}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## For one-way between subjects designs, partial eta squared is equivalent
##   to eta squared. Returning eta squared.
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
## # Effect Size for ANOVA
## 
## Parameter  |   η² |       95% CI | Interpretation
## -------------------------------------------------
## AgeSubject | 0.50 | [0.48, 1.00] |          large
## 
## - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
## - Interpretation rule: field2013
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{\texorpdfstring{\(\omega^{2}\) (omega squared)}{\textbackslash omega\^{}\{2\} (omega squared)}}\label{omega2-omega-squared}

\(\omega^{2}\) (omega squared): Provides a relatively unbiased estimate of
the variance explained in the population by a predictor variable. It
takes random error into account more so than eta squared, which is
incredibly biased to be too large. The range is from 0 to 1 and it sums
up to 1.

It is computed as:

\(\omega^{2}=\frac{SS_{model}-(df_{model}\ast MS_{error})}{SS_{total}+MS_{error}}\)

Where:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(SS_{model}\) is the sum of squares of the model
\item
  \(SS_{total}\) is the total sum of squares
\item
  \(df_{model}\) is the degrees of freedom of the model
\item
  \(MS_{error}\) is the mean square of the error.
\end{itemize}

To obtain it directly from the model, we can use the function
\texttt{omega\_squared()} from the package \texttt{effectsize} and specify
\texttt{partial\ =\ FALSE}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# omega squared}
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{aov}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{omega\_squared}\NormalTok{(., }\AttributeTok{partial =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{interpret\_omega\_squared}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)
## 
## Parameter  |   ω² |       95% CI | Interpretation
## -------------------------------------------------
## AgeSubject | 0.50 | [0.48, 1.00] |          large
## 
## - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
## - Interpretation rule: field2013
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{\texorpdfstring{Partial \(\omega^{2}\) (partial omega squared)}{Partial \textbackslash omega\^{}\{2\} (partial omega squared)}}\label{partial-omega2-partial-omega-squared}

Partial \(\omega^{2}\) (omega squared): ``proportion of total variation
attributable to the factor, partialling out (excluding) other factors
from the total non error variation''. The range is from 0 to 1 and it
sums up to more than 1 (except in one-way ANOVA). It is the equivalent
of partial eta-squared but as an unbiased measure. It is computed as:

\(\omega^{2}p=\frac{df_{factor}\ast MS_{factor}-MS_{error})}{df_{factor}\ast MS_{factor}+df_{total}- df_{factor}\ast MS_{error})}\)

Where:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(df_{factor}\) is the degrees of freedom of the factor
\item
  \(MS_{factor}\) is the mean square of the factor
\item
  \(df_{total}\) is the total degrees of freedom
\item
  \(MS_{error}\) is the mean square of the error.
\end{itemize}

To obtain it directly from the model, we can use the function
\texttt{omega\_squared()} from the package \texttt{effectsize} and specify
\texttt{partial\ =\ TRUE}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# omega squared partial}
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{aov}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{omega\_squared}\NormalTok{(., }\AttributeTok{partial =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{interpret\_omega\_squared}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## For one-way between subjects designs, partial omega squared is
##   equivalent to omega squared. Returning omega squared.
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
## # Effect Size for ANOVA
## 
## Parameter  |   ω² |       95% CI | Interpretation
## -------------------------------------------------
## AgeSubject | 0.50 | [0.48, 1.00] |          large
## 
## - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
## - Interpretation rule: field2013
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{Odds ratio}\label{odds-ratio}

We will see in the \textbf{sections} \ref{GLM} \textbf{and} \ref{GLMM} that we
use odds ratio as an exponentiation of the logodds (logit) coefficients.
Odds ratios can be interpreted as the odds for an event to occur. In
comparison to the logodds (logit) scale, which spans -6 and 6 (well
\(-\infty\) - \(\infty\)), odds ratio are very (very high) and can reach 999
for a logodds of 6.9. Of course, in some cases, odds ratio are not easy
to interpret, and it is often ``easier'' to transform the logodds into
proportions. See this \href{https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/faq/general/faq-how-do-i-interpret-odds-ratios-in-logistic-regression/}{excellent
link}
where you can understand the links better.

\subsection{Power analysis and sample size}\label{power-analysis-and-sample-size}

Usually, when we design an experiment, we always ask the question: what
is the optimal sample size to use so that I have confidence in the
results I will obtain? To answer this question, we usually say: well it
all depends on your discipline and what is feasible for a particular
study. However, this can easily lead to misconceptions and issues in
designing our studies and more importantly, in the interpretation of the
results!

Hence, we demonstrate in the following power analysis and the sample
size. These two are crucial as they are interlinked. We saw in
\textbf{section} \ref{errors} that there are four types of errors, with
\textbf{Type M} and \textbf{Type S} depending heavily on the power and on the
sample size.

We use the package \texttt{pwr}, which allows us to compute both power and
sample size (but not at the same time!!). Looking at the \href{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pwr/vignettes/pwr-vignette.html}{vignette of
the \texttt{pwr}
package},
they cite the various functions available, such as:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{pwr.p.test}: one-sample proportion test
\item
  \texttt{pwr.2p.test}: two-sample proportion test
\item
  \texttt{pwr.2p2n.test}: two-sample proportion test (unequal sample sizes)
\item
  \texttt{pwr.t.test}: two-sample, one-sample and paired t-tests
\item
  \texttt{pwr.t2n.test}: two-sample t-tests (unequal sample sizes)
\item
  \texttt{pwr.anova.test}: one-way balanced ANOVA
\item
  \texttt{pwr.r.test}: correlation test
\item
  \texttt{pwr.chisq.test}: chi-squared test (goodness of fit and association)
\item
  \texttt{pwr.f2.test}: test for the general linear model
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Cohen's \emph{d} interpretation rules and t.test}{Cohen's d interpretation rules and t.test}}\label{cohens-d-interpretation-rules-and-t.test}

Based on J. Cohen (1988) rule of thumb, we can interpret Cohen's \emph{d}
effect size measure as:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  d \textless{} 0.2 - Very small
\item
  0.2 \textless= d \textless{} 0.5 - Small
\item
  0.5 \textless= d \textless{} 0.8 - Medium
\item
  d \textgreater= 0.8 - Large
\end{itemize}

We can use the function \texttt{pwr.t.test()} to compute the power of a t.test.

\paragraph{pwr.t.test - one-sample and two-sample t tests for means}\label{pwr.t.test---one-sample-and-two-sample-t-tests-for-means}

Based on the example below, we know that the variance between the two age groups with respect to RTlexdec is significantly different; meaning that there is no equality of variance in this case. This is important to know to be able to compute the t.test appropriately.

Here are the results of the t.test between the two groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{t.test}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{var.equal =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  RTlexdec by AgeSubject
## t = 67.468, df = 4534.6, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group old and group young is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.2152787 0.2281642
## sample estimates:
##   mean in group old mean in group young 
##            6.660958            6.439237
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{Cohen's \emph{d} effect size}{Cohen's d effect size}}\label{cohens-d-effect-size}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{cohens\_d}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{interpret\_cohens\_d}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Cohen's d |       95% CI | Interpretation
## -----------------------------------------
## 2.00      | [1.93, 2.07] |          large
## 
## - Estimated using pooled SD.
## - Interpretation rule: cohen1988
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{cohen.ES}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{test =} \StringTok{"t"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{size =} \StringTok{"large"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Conventional effect size from Cohen (1982) 
## 
##            test = t
##            size = large
##     effect.size = 0.8
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{pwr.t.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n =} \DecValTok{2284}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{d =} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sig.level =} \FloatTok{2.2e{-}16}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 2284
##               d = 2
##       sig.level = 2.2e-16
##           power = 1
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group
\end{verbatim}

The results here show that with a sample size of 2284, a large effect size of 2 and a significance level of 2.2e-16, we have a power of 1 (or 100\%). This is a massive power and effect size, but we know that the results are inflated de to not using a mixed effects model.

Now, let's imagine we use another sample.

We're interested to know if there is a difference in the mean reaction time in a lexical decision task between young and old participants. Let's say we randomly ask 30 young and 30 old participants to perform the test and and calculate the mean reaction time for each group. We'll test for a difference in means using a two-sample t-test.

How powerful is this experiment if we want to detect a ``medium'' effect in either direction with a significance level of 0.001?

Unfortunately, we don't have any idea what the number of participants in the \texttt{english} dataset. It is composed of 2284 monomorphemic English nouns and verbs that are averaged across old and young subjects.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{cohen.ES}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{test =} \StringTok{"t"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{size =} \StringTok{"large"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Conventional effect size from Cohen (1982) 
## 
##            test = t
##            size = large
##     effect.size = 0.8
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{pwr.t.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n =} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{d =} \FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sig.level =} \FloatTok{0.01}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 30
##               d = 0.8
##       sig.level = 0.01
##           power = 0.6677563
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group
\end{verbatim}

The power is only at 66.78\%! Not very powerful. How many students should we observe for a test with 80\% power?

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{pwr.t.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{d =} \FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{power =} \FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sig.level =} \FloatTok{0.01}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 38.18831
##               d = 0.8
##       sig.level = 0.01
##           power = 0.8
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group
\end{verbatim}

We need at least 38 students per group. If we lower our p value, the sample size will increase drastically

\paragraph{Plots}\label{plots}

The \texttt{pwr} package comes with a handy plotting function that we can use to evaluate the impact of the increase in power, effect size and sample size for a specific p value

\subparagraph{p \textless{} 0.05}\label{p-0.05}

What if we use a specific p value \textless{} 0.05 and a power of 0.80? How does the change in effect size impact the sample size? We simulate variable effect size measures at 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 and 2 based on the interpretation above.

Based on J. Cohen (1988) rule of thumb, we can interpret Cohen's \emph{d}
effect size measure as:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  d \textless{} 0.2 - Very small
\item
  0.2 \textless= d \textless{} 0.5 - Small
\item
  0.5 \textless= d \textless{} 0.8 - Medium
\item
  d \textgreater= 0.8 - Large
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p.out }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{pwr.t.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{d =} \FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{power =} \FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sig.level =} \FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{p.out}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}

##       sig.level = 0.05
##           power = 0.8
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group
\end{verbatim}
