\subsubsection{Linear model}\label{linear-model-1}

\paragraph{General example}\label{general-example}

We borrow from the vignette of the \texttt{pwr} package an example of a linear
model.

\subparagraph{Power of the test}\label{power-of-the-test}

We want to compute the power we have with a sample size of 40 words, an
effect size of 0.3 and a significance level of 0.001.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{pwr.f2.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{u =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{v =} \DecValTok{40} \SpecialCharTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1} \SpecialCharTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{f2 =} \FloatTok{0.3}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1} \SpecialCharTok{{-}} \FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{sig.level =} \FloatTok{0.001}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Multiple regression power calculation 
## 
##               u = 1
##               v = 38
##              f2 = 0.4285714
##       sig.level = 0.001
##           power = 0.7104043
\end{verbatim}

Where:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  u = number of predictors
\item
  v = degrees of freedom of the residuals (n - u - 1)
\item
  f2 = effect size (Cohen's f2)
\item
  sig.level = significance level (alpha)
\end{itemize}

\subparagraph{Sample size}\label{sample-size}

We want to compute the sample size needed to have a power of 0.8, with a
significance level of 0.001 and an effect size of 0.3 (medium effect
size according to Cohen's conventions).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{pwr.f2.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{u =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{f2 =} \FloatTok{0.3}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1} \SpecialCharTok{{-}} \FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{sig.level =} \FloatTok{0.001}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{power =} \FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Multiple regression power calculation 
## 
##               u = 1
##               v = 43.35263
##              f2 = 0.4285714
##       sig.level = 0.001
##           power = 0.8
\end{verbatim}

Where:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  u = number of predictors
\item
  f2 = effect size (Cohen's f2)
\item
  sig.level = significance level (alpha)
\item
  power = desired power (1 - beta)
\end{itemize}

Recall \(n = v + u + 1\). Therefore, we need 43.35263 + 1 + 1 = 45.35263
\textasciitilde{} \textbf{45 words}.

\paragraph{Using our LM model}\label{using-our-lm-model}

In our case, we use the dataset \texttt{english} from the \texttt{languageR} package.
We used AgeSubject as our predictor to predict RTlexdec. What if we want
to compute the power of our model that we ran previously? Here is the
summary of our model

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)      6.660958   0.002324 2866.44   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubjectyoung -0.221721   0.003286  -67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{Power analysis from our model}\label{power-analysis-from-our-model}

Recall that the F test has numerator and denominator degrees of freedom.
The numerator degrees of freedom, \texttt{u}, is the number of coefficients
you'll have in your model (minus the intercept).

The effect size, \texttt{f2}, is \(R^{2}/(1 - R^{2})\), where \(R^{2}\) is the
coefficient of determination, aka the ``proportion of variance
explained''. To determine effect size you hypothesize the proportion of
variance your model explains, or the \(R^{2}\).

Once we computed these three values, we can compute the power of our
model based on its summary.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{fstatistic[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{v }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{fstatistic[}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{f2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{r.squared}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1} \SpecialCharTok{{-}} \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{r.squared)}
\CommentTok{\# p.value \textless{}{-} summary(model)$coefficients[2,4]}
\NormalTok{p.value }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FloatTok{0.0001}
\NormalTok{pwrModel }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{pwr.f2.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{u =}\NormalTok{ u, }\AttributeTok{v =}\NormalTok{ v, }\AttributeTok{f2 =}\NormalTok{ f2, }\AttributeTok{sig.level =}\NormalTok{ p.value)}
\NormalTok{pwrModel}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Multiple regression power calculation 
## 
##               u = 1
##               v = 4566
##              f2 = 0.9969247
##       sig.level = 1e-04
##           power = 1
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{Sample size}\label{sample-size-1}

For the optimal sample size, we use the same values for \texttt{u}, \texttt{f2} and
\texttt{p.value} as above, but we specify the power we want to have. Here, we
use the power we obtained from our model above.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pwrSample }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{pwr.f2.test}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{u =}\NormalTok{ u, }\AttributeTok{f2 =}\NormalTok{ f2, }\AttributeTok{sig.level =}\NormalTok{ p.value, }\AttributeTok{power =}\NormalTok{ pwrModel}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{power)}
\NormalTok{pwrSample}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##      Multiple regression power calculation 
## 
##               u = 1
##               v = 1e+09
##              f2 = 0.9969247
##       sig.level = 1e-04
##           power = 1
\end{verbatim}

Based on the output, we can compute the optimal sample size needed for
our model as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ pwrSample}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{v }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ u }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{n}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## numdf 
## 1e+09
\end{verbatim}

The optimal sample size to reach this level of power is \textbf{1,000,000,000
words}! BUT we do not have that many words in our dataset. This is kind
of telling us that there are serious issues in our model. In fact, we
see that we have a power of 1, which is very high power. However, we
know very well that our linear model is inaccurate. We did not tell our
model that the data comes from multiple words, and that we really need
to compute a mixed effects regression (see \textbf{Section} \ref{LMM} from
\textbf{chapter} \ref{Random-LMM-GLMM-CLMM-GAMM}).

\section{Correlation tests}\label{correlation-tests}

\subsection{Correlation does not imply causation!}\label{correlation-does-not-imply-causation}

There is a general misconception that when one conducts a correlation
test (see below), we can explain causation. An excellent example is
borrowed from
\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_does_not_imply_causation\#}{wikipedia}.
It is not because two variables are correlated (positively or
negatively) that one explains the reasons behind the second!

If you want to evaluate the cause of an effect then inferential
statistics that we cover after the correlation tests are the ones to go
for.

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{images/Illiterate_Dinos.jpg}}

\subsection{Basic correlations}\label{basic-correlations}

Let us start with a basic correlation test. We want to evaluate if two
numeric variables are correlated with each other.

We use the function \texttt{cor} to obtain the pearson correlation and
\texttt{cor.test} to run a basic correlation test on our data with significance
testing

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{cor}\NormalTok{(english}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{RTlexdec, english}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{RTnaming, }\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"pearson"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.7587033
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{cor.test}\NormalTok{(english}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{RTlexdec, english}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{RTnaming)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  english$RTlexdec and english$RTnaming
## t = 78.699, df = 4566, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.7461195 0.7707453
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.7587033
\end{verbatim}

What these results are telling us? There is a positive correlation
between \texttt{RTlexdec} and \texttt{RTnaming}. The correlation coefficient (R²) is
0.76 (limits between -1 and 1). This correlation is statistically
significant with a t value of 78.699, degrees of freedom of 4566 and a
p-value \textless{} 2.2e-16.

What are the degrees of freedom? These relate to number of total
observations - number of comparisons. Here we have 4568 observations in
the dataset, and two comparisons, hence 4568 - 2 = 4566.

For the p value, there is a threshold we usually use. This threshold is
p = 0.05. This threshold means we have a minimum to consider any
difference as significant or not. 0.05 means that we have a probability
to find a significant difference that is at 5\% or lower. IN our case,
the p value is lower that 2.2e-16. How to interpret this number? this
tells us to add 15 0s before the 2!! i.e., 0.0000000000000002. This
probability is very (very!!) low. So we conclude that there is a
statistically significant correlation between the two variables.

The formula to calculate the t value is below.

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{images/t-score.jpg}}

x̄ = sample mean μ0 = population mean s = sample standard deviation n =
sample size

The p value is influenced by various factors, number of observations,
strength of the difference, mean values, etc.. You should always be
careful with interpreting p values taking everything else into account.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using the package \texttt{corrplot}}{Using the package corrplot}}\label{using-the-package-corrplot}

Above, we did a correlation test on two predictors. What if we want to
obtain a nice plot of all numeric predictors and add significance
levels?

\subsubsection{Correlation plots}\label{correlation-plots}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{corr }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} 
\NormalTok{  english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{where}\NormalTok{(is.numeric)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{cor}\NormalTok{()}
\FunctionTok{corrplot}\NormalTok{(corr, }\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}ellipse\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}upper\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-151-1.pdf}}

\subsubsection{More advanced}\label{more-advanced}

Let's first compute the correlations between all numeric variables and
plot these with the p values

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\# correlation using "corrplot"}
\DocumentationTok{\#\# based on the function \textasciigrave{}rcorr\textquotesingle{} from the \textasciigrave{}Hmisc\textasciigrave{} package}
\DocumentationTok{\#\# Need to change dataframe into a matrix}
\NormalTok{corr }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} 
\NormalTok{  english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{where}\NormalTok{(is.numeric)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{data.matrix}\NormalTok{(english) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{rcorr}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"pearson"}\NormalTok{)}
\CommentTok{\# use corrplot to obtain a nice correlation plot!}
\FunctionTok{corrplot}\NormalTok{(corr}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{r, }\AttributeTok{p.mat =}\NormalTok{ corr}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{P,}
         \AttributeTok{addCoef.col =} \StringTok{"black"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{diag =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"upper"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{tl.srt =} \DecValTok{55}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/fig.width==14-1.pdf}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{mean =} \FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec),}
            \AttributeTok{sd =} \FunctionTok{sd}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 2 x 3
##   AgeSubject  mean    sd
##   <fct>      <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 old         6.66 0.116
## 2 young       6.44 0.106
\end{verbatim}

\section{Linear Models}\label{LM}

Up to now, we have looked at descriptive statistics, and evaluated
summaries, correlations in the data (with p values).

We are now interested in looking at group differences. But before moving
into linear models, let's assume we simply wanted to use a student's
t.test to evaluate the differences between two groups. In our case, we
have two age groups within the variable \texttt{AgeSubject} (young vs old).
Before running a t.test, there are some assumptions one needs to take
into account:

\subsection{Normality of distribution}\label{normality-of-distribution}

\subsubsection{Shapiro test}\label{shapiro-test}

To check normality of distribution, we use the \texttt{shapiro.test} on the
numeric outcome. Given that our predictor now has two levels.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{shapiro.test}\NormalTok{(english}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{RTlexdec)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  english$RTlexdec
## W = 0.98595, p-value < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

How to interpret this statistically significant result? This tells us
that the distribution of the data is statistically different from a
normal distribution.

\subsubsection{Density plot}\label{density-plot}

We can also use a density plot to evaluate normality. The results show
that both levels have bell shaped distributions but they are both skewed
to the right (positively skewed data). See \href{https://www.cambridgemaths.org/blogs/skewed-usage-skewed-distribution/}{this
website}
for a nice example of left and right skwed data distributions.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec))}\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_density}\NormalTok{()}\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{facet\_wrap}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-154-1.pdf}}

\subsection{Homogeneity of variance}\label{homogeneity-of-variance}

If our data were normally distributed, we can use the \texttt{bartlett} test.
If our data were non-normally distributed, we would use the Levene Test
(either with \texttt{var.test} from base-R or \texttt{leveneTest} from the car package
We can check both.

\subsubsection{Bartlett test}\label{bartlett-test}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{bartlett.test}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances
## 
## data:  RTlexdec by AgeSubject
## Bartlett's K-squared = 15.883, df = 1, p-value = 6.737e-05
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Levene test}\label{levene-test}

\paragraph{Base R}\label{base-r}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{var.test}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  F test to compare two variances
## 
## data:  RTlexdec by AgeSubject
## F = 1.1817, num df = 2283, denom df = 2283, p-value = 6.737e-05
## alternative hypothesis: true ratio of variances is not equal to 1
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  1.088581 1.282737
## sample estimates:
## ratio of variances 
##           1.181678
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{From the \texttt{car} package}{From the car package}}\label{from-the-car-package}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
\NormalTok{  car}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{leveneTest}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
##         Df F value  Pr(>F)  
## group    1  5.1615 0.02314 *
##       4566                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
\end{verbatim}

In all cases, the statistically significant result indicates that there
is evidence that the variance of two levels of the factor \texttt{AgeSubject}
is statistically significant; i.e., the variances are not equal. This is
important as we will use this in our t-test later on.

\subsection{First steps}\label{first-steps-3}

Up to now, we have looked at descriptive statistics, and evaluated
summaries, correlations in the data (with p values), and checked the
normality of distribution of our data.

We are now interested in looking at group differences.

Let us start with a simple t-test

\subsubsection{T-test}\label{t-test}

We then run a t-test on the data. We specify the formula as \texttt{y\ \textasciitilde{}\ x} and
add \texttt{var.equal\ =\ FALSE} (based on the normality tests above)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{t.test}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{var.equal =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  RTlexdec by AgeSubject
## t = 67.468, df = 4534.6, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group old and group young is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.2152787 0.2281642
## sample estimates:
##   mean in group old mean in group young 
##            6.660958            6.439237
\end{verbatim}

To interpret the t-test, we say that there is evidence for a
statistically significant difference between the two groups: \texttt{young}
and \texttt{old}: \texttt{t(4534.6)\ =\ 67.468,\ p\ \textless{}\ 2.2e-16}. The mean of
\texttt{RTLexdec} for the young group is significantly lower than that of the
old group.

\subsubsection{Linear Model}\label{linear-model-2}

Let us run a linear model on the same data

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)      6.660958   0.002324 2866.44   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubjectyoung -0.221721   0.003286  -67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

Any comments? discuss with your neighbour.

The results of the linear model are exactly the same, albeit with a
difference in the sign of the difference. This indicates that the
\(\beta\) coefficient for \texttt{young} is significantly lower than that
of \texttt{old} by \texttt{-0.221721}: \texttt{t\ =\ -67.47,\ p\ \textless{}\ \textless{}2e-16}.

The dataset \texttt{english} contains two levels for \texttt{AgeSubject.} We will run
an ANOVA and a linear model on the data.

\subsubsection{Basic ANOVA}\label{basic-anova}

We can use the function \texttt{aov} to run an Analysis of Variance on the full
dataset

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{aov}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## AgeSubject     1  56.14   56.14    4552 <2e-16 ***
## Residuals   4566  56.31    0.01                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Linear model}\label{linear-model-3}

We can use the function \texttt{lm} to run a linear model

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)      6.660958   0.002324 2866.44   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubjectyoung -0.221721   0.003286  -67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

But wait\ldots{} How is the linear model comparable to the analysis of
variance we ran above? This linear model derives the analysis of
variance we saw above, use \texttt{anova} on your linear model..

Here are the results of the initial Analysis of variance:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{aov}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## AgeSubject     1  56.14   56.14    4552 <2e-16 ***
## Residuals   4566  56.31    0.01                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
\end{verbatim}

And here are the results of the linear model with the \texttt{anova} function

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{anova}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: RTlexdec
##              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
## AgeSubject    1 56.141  56.141    4552 < 2.2e-16 ***
## Residuals  4566 56.314   0.012                      
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
\end{verbatim}

They are exactly the same\ldots{} The underlying of an Analysis of variance
is a linear model. We will continue with a linear model to understand it
better

\subsection{Introduction to Linear models}\label{introduction-to-linear-models}

The basic assumption of a Linear model is to create a regression
analysis on the data. We have an outcome (or dependent variable) and a
predictor (or an independent variable). The formula of a linear model is
as follows \texttt{outcome\ \textasciitilde{}\ predictor} that can be read as ``outcome as a
function of the predictor''. We can add ``1'' to specify an intercept, but
this is by default added to the model

\subsubsection{Model estimation}\label{model-estimation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeSubject =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{mdl.lm }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\CommentTok{\#lm(RTlexdec \textasciitilde{} AgeSubject, data = english)}
\NormalTok{mdl.lm }\CommentTok{\#also print(mdl.lm)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = .)
## 
## Coefficients:
##   (Intercept)  AgeSubjectold  
##        6.4392         0.2217
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   6.439237   0.002324 2771.03   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubjectold 0.221721   0.003286   67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Role of coding schemes}\label{role-of-coding-schemes}

\subsubsection{Intro}\label{intro-1}

There are other coding schemes that can be used. See Schad et al.
(2020): ``How to capitalize on a priori contrasts in linear (mixed)
models: A tutorial''. \textbf{Journal of Memory and Language},vol.~110,
104038.

We have:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The treatment coding
\item
  The contrast or sum coding
\item
  The polynomial coding
\item
  The Repeated coding
\item
  The helmert coding
\end{enumerate}

The first two are the most commonly used coding schemes, but see the
paper for why one can use the others.

\subsubsection{Treatment coding}\label{treatment-coding}

By default, \texttt{R} uses a treatment coding scheme. By this we mean that the
intercept has the outcome of a specific level in the dataset (usually,
the first in alphabetical order, unless you have changed that!). In our
example above, we changed the reference level of the variable
\texttt{AgeSubject} to be ``young'' vs ``old''. What we see as an result in our LM
is the intercept (=Young) vs ``AgeSubjectold''. This will mean we are
looking at the difference between the reference level and all other
levels.

The code below allows you to see what the coding scheme is.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject}

\FunctionTok{contrasts}\NormalTok{(english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject2) }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{contr.treatment}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{contrasts}\NormalTok{(english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject2) }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##       2
## young 0
## old   1
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.lm.T }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject2, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\CommentTok{\#lm(RTlexdec \textasciitilde{} AgeSubject, data = english)}
\NormalTok{mdl.lm.T }\CommentTok{\#also print(mdl.lm)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject2, data = .)
## 
## Coefficients:
##  (Intercept)  AgeSubject22  
##       6.4392        0.2217
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm.T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject2, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  6.439237   0.002324 2771.03   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubject22 0.221721   0.003286   67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Contrast (or sum) coding}\label{contrast-or-sum-coding}

\paragraph{Default}\label{default}

Let's change the coding scheme and see the difference in the output.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeSubject2 =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject2, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{)))}

\FunctionTok{contrasts}\NormalTok{(english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject2) }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{contr.sum}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{contrasts}\NormalTok{(english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##       [,1]
## old      1
## young   -1
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.lm.C }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject2, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\CommentTok{\#lm(RTlexdec \textasciitilde{} AgeSubject, data = english)}
\NormalTok{mdl.lm.C }\CommentTok{\#also print(mdl.lm)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject2, data = .)
## 
## Coefficients:
##  (Intercept)  AgeSubject21  
##       6.5501        0.1109
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm.C)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject2, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  6.550097   0.001643 3986.29   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubject21 0.110861   0.001643   67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

With contrast (or sum) coding, the intercept is almost the same as
before (treatment = 6.439237 vs contrast = 6.550097). The intercept is
now the average of all of the data points

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{meanRTlexdec =} \FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(meanRTlexdec) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##    meanRTlexdec
## 1      6.550097
## 2      6.550097
## 3      6.550097
## 4      6.550097
## 5      6.550097
## 6      6.550097
## 7      6.550097
## 8      6.550097
## 9      6.550097
## 10     6.550097
\end{verbatim}

The coefficient for \texttt{old} is different. It is now nearly half of that in
the treatment coding (0.221721 vs 0.110861). Why is this the case? In
treatment coding, the distance between old and young was of 1 (1- 0 =
1), in contrast coding, it is of 2 (1 - -1 = 2). The coefficient of the
intercept is exactly the same; for the second, it is half of the one
above (0.221721 / 1 = 0.221721; 0.221721 / 2 = 0.110861)!

How to interpret the coefficient for the level ``old''? It is the distance
from the average!

Let's change slightly the coding scheme

\paragraph{Modified}\label{modified}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeSubject2 =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{)))}

\FunctionTok{contrasts}\NormalTok{(english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject2) }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{contrasts}\NormalTok{(english2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{AgeSubject2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##       [,1]
## young -0.5
## old    0.5
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.lmC}\FloatTok{.2} \OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject2, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\CommentTok{\#lm(RTlexdec \textasciitilde{} AgeSubject, data = english)}
\NormalTok{mdl.lmC}\FloatTok{.2} \CommentTok{\#also print(mdl.lmC.2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject2, data = .)
## 
## Coefficients:
##  (Intercept)  AgeSubject21  
##       6.5501        0.2217
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.lmC}\FloatTok{.2}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject2, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  6.550097   0.001643 3986.29   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubject21 0.221721   0.003286   67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

Our intercept is still the average of all datapoints of the dependent
variable; that of ``old'' is now at 0.221721 as expected. The distance
between young and old is of 1 (0.5 - -0.5 = 1).

When and why do we use the different coding schemes? We use it to make
the intercept more interpretable. This is especially the case when
having more than two categorical predictors, or interactions between a
numeric and a categorical predictor. Read the paper and the Bodo
Winter's book for more details.

\subsection{Further steps}\label{further-steps}

\subsubsection{Tidying the output}\label{tidying-the-output}

We use our original model with treatment coding.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# from library(broom)}
\FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(term, estimate) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{estimate =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(estimate, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 2 x 2
##   term          estimate
##   <chr>            <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)      6.44 
## 2 AgeSubjectold    0.222
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mycoefE }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{pull}\NormalTok{(estimate)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Obtaining mean values from our model

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#old}
\NormalTok{mycoefE[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 6.439237
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#young}
\NormalTok{mycoefE[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ mycoefE[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 6.660958
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Nice table of our model summary}\label{nice-table-of-our-model-summary}

We can also obtain a nice table of our model summary. We can use the
package \texttt{knitr} or \texttt{xtable}

\paragraph{Directly from model summary}\label{directly-from-model-summary}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{kable}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{coef, }\AttributeTok{digits =} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tabular}{l|r|r|r|r}
\hline
  & Estimate & Std. Error & t value & Pr(>|t|)\\
\hline
(Intercept) & 6.439 & 0.002 & 2771.027 & 0\\
\hline
AgeSubjectold & 0.222 & 0.003 & 67.468 & 0\\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{From the \texttt{tidy} output}{From the tidy output}}\label{from-the-tidy-output}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.lmT }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)}
\FunctionTok{kable}\NormalTok{(mdl.lmT, }\AttributeTok{digits =} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tabular}{l|r|r|r|r}
\hline
term & estimate & std.error & statistic & p.value\\
\hline
(Intercept) & 6.439 & 0.002 & 2771.027 & 0\\
\hline
AgeSubjectold & 0.222 & 0.003 & 67.468 & 0\\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\paragraph{Model's fit}\label{models-fit}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{tab\_model}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm, }\AttributeTok{file =} \FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"outputs/mdl\_lm.html"}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{htmltools}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{includeHTML}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"outputs/mdl\_lm.html"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Dissecting the model}\label{dissecting-the-model}

Let us dissect the model. If you use ``str'', you will be able to see what
is available under our linear model. To access some info from the model

\paragraph{Residuals}\label{residuals}

What about residuals (difference between the observed value and the
estimated value of the quantity) and fitted values? This allows us to
evaluate how normal our residuals are and how different they are from a
normal distribution.

\end{Highlighting}

## # A tibble: 1 x 12
##   r.squared adj.r.squared sigma statistic p.value    df logLik    AIC    BIC
##       <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1     0.499         0.499 0.111     4552.       0     1  3558. -7111. -7092.
## # i 3 more variables: deviance <dbl>, df.residual <int>, nobs <int>
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{Significance testing}\label{significance-testing}

Are the above informative? of course not directly. If we want to test
for overall significance of model. We run a null model (aka intercept
only) and compare models.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.lm.Null }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\NormalTok{mdl.comp }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{anova}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm.Null, mdl.lm)}
\NormalTok{mdl.comp}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: RTlexdec ~ 1
## Model 2: RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject
##   Res.Df     RSS Df Sum of Sq    F    Pr(>F)    
## 1   4567 112.456                                
## 2   4566  56.314  1    56.141 4552 < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
\end{verbatim}

The results show that adding the variable ``AgeSubject'' improves the
model fit. We can write this as follows: Model comparison showed that
the addition of AgeSubject improved the model fit when compared with an
intercept only model (\(F\)(1) =
4551.96, \emph{p} \textless{} 0) (F(1) = 4552 , p
\textless{} 2.2e-16)

\subsection{Plotting fitted values}\label{plotting-fitted-values}

Let's plot our fitted values but only for the trend line

\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}

  \FunctionTok{geom\_smooth}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =} \FunctionTok{as.numeric}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject), }\AttributeTok{y =} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)), }\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"lm"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{color =} \StringTok{"blue"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+} 
  \FunctionTok{labs}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =} \StringTok{"Age"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{y =} \StringTok{"RTLexDec"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{title =} \StringTok{"Boxplot and predicted trend line"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{subtitle =} \StringTok{"with ggplot2"}\NormalTok{) }

\subsubsection{Add significance levels and trend line on a plot?}\label{add-significance-levels-and-trend-line-on-a-plot}

We can use the p values generated from either our linear model to add
significance levels on a plot. We use the code from above and add the
significance level. We also add a trend line

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec))}\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{y =} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)), }\AttributeTok{color =} \StringTok{"blue"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme\_bw}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{+} \FunctionTok{theme}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{text =} \FunctionTok{element\_text}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{size =} \DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_smooth}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =} \FunctionTok{as.numeric}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject), }\AttributeTok{y =} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)), }\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"lm"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{color =} \StringTok{"blue"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
    \FunctionTok{labs}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =} \StringTok{"Species"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{y =} \StringTok{"Length"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{title =} \StringTok{"Boxplot raw data, predicted means (in blue) and trend line"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{subtitle =} \StringTok{"with significance testing"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
    \FunctionTok{geom\_signif}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{comparison =} \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"old"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"young"}\NormalTok{)), }
              \AttributeTok{map\_signif\_level =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{test =} \ControlFlowTok{function}\NormalTok{(a, b) \{}
                \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{p.value =} \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{coefficients[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{])\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{What about pairwise comparison?}\label{what-about-pairwise-comparison}

When having three of more levels in our predictor, we can use pairwise
comparisons, with corrections to evaluate differences between each
level.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.lm)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25776 -0.08339 -0.01669  0.06921  0.52685 
## 
## Coefficients:
##               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   6.439237   0.002324 2771.03   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubjectold 0.221721   0.003286   67.47   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1111 on 4566 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4992, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4991 
## F-statistic:  4552 on 1 and 4566 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.lm }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{emmeans}\NormalTok{(pairwise }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject, }\AttributeTok{adjust =} \StringTok{"fdr"}\NormalTok{) }\OtherTok{{-}\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{ mdl.emmeans}
\NormalTok{mdl.emmeans}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## $emmeans
##  AgeSubject emmean      SE   df lower.CL upper.CL
##  young       6.439 0.00232 4566    6.435    6.444
##  old         6.661 0.00232 4566    6.656    6.666
## 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## 
## $contrasts
##  contrast    estimate      SE   df t.ratio p.value
##  young - old   -0.222 0.00329 4566 -67.468  <.0001
\end{verbatim}

How to interpret the output? Discuss with your neighbour and share with
the group.

Hint\ldots{} Look at the emmeans values for each level of our factor
``AgeSubject'' and the contrasts.

\subsection{Multiple predictors?}\label{multiple-predictors}

Linear models require a numeric outcome, but the predictor can be either
numeric or a factor. We can have more than one predictor. The only issue
is that this complicates the interpretation of results

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject }\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{ WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = RTlexdec ~ AgeSubject * WordCategory, data = .)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.25079 -0.08273 -0.01516  0.06940  0.52285 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                                Estimate Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)                    6.664955   0.002911 2289.950   <2e-16 ***
## AgeSubjectyoung               -0.220395   0.004116  -53.545   <2e-16 ***
## WordCategoryV                 -0.010972   0.004822   -2.275   0.0229 *  
## AgeSubjectyoung:WordCategoryV -0.003642   0.006820   -0.534   0.5934    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1109 on 4564 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.5008, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5005 
## F-statistic:  1526 on 3 and 4564 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
\end{verbatim}

And with an Anova

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{english }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{lm}\NormalTok{(RTlexdec }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ AgeSubject }\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{ WordCategory, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{anova}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: RTlexdec
##                           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq   F value    Pr(>F)    
## AgeSubject                 1 56.141  56.141 4564.2810 < 2.2e-16 ***
## WordCategory               1  0.173   0.173   14.0756 0.0001778 ***
## AgeSubject:WordCategory    1  0.004   0.004    0.2851 0.5933724    
## Residuals               4564 56.138   0.012                        
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
\end{verbatim}

The results above tell us that all predictors used are significantly
different.

\section{Generalised Linear Models}\label{GLM}

Here we will look at an example when the outcome is binary. This
simulated data is structured as follows. We asked one participant to
listen to 165 sentences, and to judge whether these are ``grammatical'' or
``ungrammatical''. There were 105 sentences that were ``grammatical'' and 60
``ungrammatical''. Responses varied, with 110 ``yes'' responses and 55 ``no''
responses, spread across the grammatical.

This fictitious example can apply in any other situation. Let's think
Geography: 165 lands: 105 ``flat'' and 60 ``non-flat'', etc. This applies to
any case where you need to ``categorise'' the outcome into two groups.

\subsection{Load and summaries}\label{load-and-summaries}

Let's create this dataset from scratch (you can load the
``grammatical.csv file as well) and do some basic summaries

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{grammatical }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{as.data.frame}\NormalTok{(}
  \FunctionTok{cbind}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grammaticality"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grammatical"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{rep}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grammatical"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{105}\NormalTok{),}
                             \StringTok{"ungrammatical"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{rep}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"ungrammatical"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{)),}
        \StringTok{"response"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"yes"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{rep}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{),}
                       \StringTok{"no"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{rep}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{),}
                       \StringTok{"yes"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{rep}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{),}
                       \StringTok{"no"} \OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{rep}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{))),}
  \AttributeTok{row.names =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##    grammaticality response
## 1     grammatical      yes
## 2     grammatical      yes
## 3     grammatical      yes
## 4     grammatical      yes
## 5     grammatical      yes
## 6     grammatical      yes
## 7     grammatical      yes
## 8     grammatical      yes
## 9     grammatical      yes
## 10    grammatical      yes
## 11    grammatical      yes
## 12    grammatical      yes
## 13    grammatical      yes
## 14    grammatical      yes
## 15    grammatical      yes
## 16    grammatical      yes
## 17    grammatical      yes
## 18    grammatical      yes
## 19    grammatical      yes
## 20    grammatical      yes
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{str}\NormalTok{(grammatical)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 'data.frame':    165 obs. of  2 variables:
##  $ grammaticality: chr  "grammatical" "grammatical" "grammatical" "grammatical" ...
##  $ response      : chr  "yes" "yes" "yes" "yes" ...
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(grammatical)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##   grammaticality response
## 1    grammatical      yes
## 2    grammatical      yes
## 3    grammatical      yes
## 4    grammatical      yes
## 5    grammatical      yes
## 6    grammatical      yes
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(grammatical}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{response, grammatical}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{grammaticality)}
\end{Highlighting}

##      
##       grammatical ungrammatical

\end{verbatim}

\subsection{GLM - Categorical predictors}\label{glm---categorical-predictors}

Let's run a first GLM (Generalised Linear Model). A GLM uses a special
family ``binomial'' as it assumes the outcome has a binomial distribution.
In general, results from a Logistic Regression are close to what we get
from SDT (see above).

To run the results, we will change the reference level for both response
and grammaticality. The basic assumption about GLM is that we start with
our reference level being the ``no'' responses to the ``ungrammatical''
category. Any changes to this reference will be seen in the coefficients
as ``yes'' responses to the ``grammatical'' category.

\subsubsection{Model estimation and results}\label{model-estimation-and-results}

The results below show the logodds for our model.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{grammatical }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{response =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(response, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{grammaticality =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(grammaticality, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"ungrammatical"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"grammatical"}\NormalTok{)))}

\NormalTok{grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(grammaticality, response) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##                response
## grammaticality   no yes
##   ungrammatical  50  10
##   grammatical     5 100
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.glm }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(response }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ grammaticality, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial)}
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = response ~ grammaticality, family = binomial, data = .)
## 
## Coefficients:
##                           Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)                -1.6094     0.3464  -4.646 3.38e-06 ***
## grammaticalitygrammatical   4.6052     0.5744   8.017 1.08e-15 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 210.050  on 164  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance:  94.271  on 163  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 98.271
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(term, estimate) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{estimate =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(estimate, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 2 x 2
##   term                      estimate
##   <chr>                        <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)                  -1.61
## 2 grammaticalitygrammatical     4.61
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# to only get the coefficients}
\NormalTok{mycoef2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{pull}\NormalTok{(estimate)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Model's fit}\label{models-fit-1}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{tab\_model}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm, }\AttributeTok{file =} \FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"outputs/mdl.glm.html"}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{htmltools}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{includeHTML}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"outputs/mdl.glm.html"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The results show that for one unit increase in the response (i.e., from
no to yes), the logodds of being ``grammatical'' is increased by
4.6051702 (the intercept shows that when the response is ``no'', the
logodds are -1.6094379). The actual logodds for the response ``yes''
to grammatical is 2.9957323

\subsubsection{Logodds to Odd ratios}\label{logodds-to-odd-ratios}

Logodds can be modified to talk about the odds of an event. For our
model above, the odds of ``grammatical'' receiving a ``no'' response is a
mere 0.2; the odds of ``grammatical'' to receive a ``yes'' is a 20; i.e., 20
times more likely

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{exp}\NormalTok{(mycoef2[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.2
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{exp}\NormalTok{(mycoef2[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ mycoef2[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 20
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{LogOdds to proportions}\label{logodds-to-proportions}

If you want to talk about the percentage ``accuracy'' of our model, then
we can transform our loggodds into proportions. This shows that the
proportion of ``grammatical'' receiving a ``yes'' response increases by 99\%
(or 95\% based on our ``true'' coefficients)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{plogis}\NormalTok{(mycoef2[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.1666667
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{plogis}\NormalTok{(mycoef2[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ mycoef2[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.952381

\subsection{GLM - Numeric predictors}\label{glm---numeric-predictors}

In this example, we will run a GLM model using a similar technique to
that used in \texttt{Al-Tamimi\ (2017)} and \texttt{Baumann\ \&\ Winter\ (2018)}. We use
the package \texttt{LanguageR} and the dataset \texttt{English}.

In the model above, we used the equation as lm(RTlexdec \textasciitilde{} AgeSubject).
We were interested in examining the impact of age of subject on reaction
time in a lexical decision task. In this section, we are interested in
understanding how reaction time allows to differentiate the participants
based on their age. We use \texttt{AgeSubject} as our outcome and \texttt{RTlexdec} as
our predictor using the equation glm(AgeSubject \textasciitilde{} RTlexdec). We usually
can use \texttt{RTlexdec} as is, but due to a possible quasi separation and the
fact that we may want to compare coefficients using multiple acoustic
metrics, we will z-score our predictor. We run below two models, with
and without z-scoring

For the glm model, we need to specify \texttt{family\ =\ "binomial"}.

\subsubsection{Without z-scoring of predictor}\label{without-z-scoring-of-predictor}

\paragraph{Model estimation}\label{model-estimation-1}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.glm2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ english2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(AgeSubject }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ RTlexdec, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =} \StringTok{"binomial"}\NormalTok{)}

\FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm2) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(term, estimate) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{estimate =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(estimate, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 2 x 2
##   term        estimate
##   <chr>          <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)   -129. 
## 2 RTlexdec        19.6
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# to only get the coefficients}
\NormalTok{mycoef2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm2) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{pull}\NormalTok{(estimate)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Signal Detection Theory}\label{STD}

\subsubsection{Rationale}\label{rationale}

We are generally interested in performance, i.e., whether the we have
``accurately'' categorised the outcome or not and at the same time want to
evaluate our biases in responses. When deciding on categories, we are
usually biased in our selection.

Let's ask the question: How many of you have a Mac laptop and how many a
Windows laptop? For those with a Mac, what was the main reason for
choosing it? Are you biased in anyway by your decision?

To correct for these biases, we use some variants from Signal Detection
Theory to obtain the true estimates without being influenced by the
biases.

\subsubsection{Running stats}\label{running-stats}

Let's do some stats on this

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& Yes & No & Total \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Grammatical (Yes Actual) & TP = 100 & FN = 5 & (Yes Actual) 105 \\
Ungrammatical (No Actual) & FP = 10 & TN = 50 & (No Actual) 60 \\
Total & (Yes Response) 110 & (No Response) 55 & 165 \\
\end{longtable}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{grammatical }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{response =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(response, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{grammaticality =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(grammaticality, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grammatical"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ungrammatical"}\NormalTok{)))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Below we obtain multiple measures}\label{below-we-obtain-multiple-measures}

\paragraph{TP, FP, FN, TN}\label{tp-fp-fn-tn}

TP = True Positive (Hit); FP = False Positive; FN = False Negative; TN =
True Negative

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{TP }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
             \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(grammaticality }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"grammatical"} \SpecialCharTok{\&}
\NormalTok{                      response }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{FN }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
             \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(grammaticality }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"grammatical"} \SpecialCharTok{\&}
\NormalTok{                      response }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{FP }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
             \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(grammaticality }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"ungrammatical"} \SpecialCharTok{\&}
\NormalTok{                      response }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{TN }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
             \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(grammaticality }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"ungrammatical"} \SpecialCharTok{\&}
\NormalTok{                      response }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{TP}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 100
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{FN}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 5
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{FP}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 10
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{TN}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 50
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{Accuracy, Error, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision, etc.}\label{accuracy-error-sensitivity-specificity-precision-etc.}

\subparagraph{Accuracy and Error}\label{accuracy-and-error}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(TP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{TN)}\SpecialCharTok{/}\FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(grammatical) }\CommentTok{\# accuracy}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.9090909
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(FP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{FN)}\SpecialCharTok{/}\FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(grammatical) }\CommentTok{\# error, also 1{-}accuracy}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.09090909
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision, etc.}\label{sensitivity-specificity-precision-etc.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# When stimulus = yes, how many times response = yes?}
\NormalTok{TP}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{(TP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{FN) }\CommentTok{\# also True Positive Rate or Specificity}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.952381
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# When stimulus = no, how many times response = yes?}
\NormalTok{FP}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{(FP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{TN) }\CommentTok{\# False Positive Rate, }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.1666667
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# When stimulus = no, how many times response = no?}
\NormalTok{TN}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{(FP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{TN) }\CommentTok{\# True Negative Rate or Sensitivity }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.8333333
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# When subject responds "yes" how many times is (s)he correct?}
\NormalTok{TP}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{(TP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{FP) }\CommentTok{\# precision}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.9090909
\end{verbatim}

\subparagraph{STD measures}\label{std-measures}

We can get various measures from Signal Detection Theory. using the
package \texttt{psycho}.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  dprime (or the sensitivity index)
\item
  beta (bias criterion, 0-1, lower = increase in ``yes'')
\item
  Aprime (estimate of discriminability, 0-1, 1 = good discrimination;
  0 at chance)
\item
  bppd (b prime prime d, -1 to 1; 0 = no bias, negative = tendency to
  respond ``yes'', positive = tendency to respond ``no'')
\item
  c (index of bias, equals to SD)
\end{itemize}

See
\href{https://www.r-bloggers.com/compute-signal-detection-theory-indices-with-r/amp/}{here}
for more details

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{psycho}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{dprime}\NormalTok{(TP, FP, FN, TN, }
               \AttributeTok{n\_targets =}\NormalTok{ TP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{FN, }
               \AttributeTok{n\_distractors =}\NormalTok{ FP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{TN,}
               \AttributeTok{adjust=}\NormalTok{F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## $dprime
## [1] 2.635813
## 
## $beta
## [1] 0.3970026
## 
## $aprime
## [1] 0.9419643
## 
## $bppd
## [1] -0.5076923
## 
## $c
## [1] -0.3504848
\end{verbatim}

The most important from above, is d-prime. This is modelling the
difference between the rate of ``True Positive'' responses and ``False
Positive'' responses in standard unit (or z-scores). The formula can be
written as:

\texttt{d\textquotesingle{}\ (d\ prime)\ =\ Z(True\ Positive\ Rate)\ -\ Z(False\ Positive\ Rate)}

\subsubsection{GLM and d prime}\label{glm-and-d-prime}

The values obtained here match those obtained from SDT. For d prime, the
difference stems from the use of the logit variant of the Binomial
family. By using a probit variant, one obtains the same values (\href{https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/r/dae/probit-regression/}{see
here} for more
details). A probit variant models the z-score differences in the outcome
and is evaluated in change in 1-standard unit. This is modelling the
change from ``ungrammatical'' ``no'' responses into ``grammatical'' ``yes''
responses in z-scores. The same conceptual underpinnings of d-prime from
Signal Detection Theory.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\# d prime}
\NormalTok{psycho}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{dprime}\NormalTok{(TP, FP, FN, TN, }
               \AttributeTok{n\_targets =}\NormalTok{ TP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{FN, }
               \AttributeTok{n\_distractors =}\NormalTok{ FP}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{TN,}
               \AttributeTok{adjust=}\NormalTok{F)}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{dprime}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 2.635813
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\# GLM with probit}
\FunctionTok{coef}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(response }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ grammaticality, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ grammatical, }\AttributeTok{family =} \FunctionTok{binomial}\NormalTok{(probit)))[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}

\subsubsection{GLM as a classification tool}\label{GLM-Classification}

The code below demonstrates the links between our GLM model and what we
had obtained above from SDT. The predictions' table shows that our GLM
was successful at obtaining prediction that are identical to our initial
data setup. Look at the table here and the table above. Once we have
created our table of outcome, we can compute percent correct, the
specificity, the sensitivity, the Kappa score, etc.. this yields the
actual value with the SD that is related to variations in responses.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\# predict(mdl.glm)\textgreater{}0.5 is identical to }
\DocumentationTok{\#\# predict(glm(response\textasciitilde{}grammaticality,data=grammatical,family = binomial),type="response")}
\NormalTok{grammatical }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{response =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(response, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{grammaticality =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(grammaticality, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grammatical"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ungrammatical"}\NormalTok{)))}



\NormalTok{mdl.glm.C }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ grammatical }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(response }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ grammaticality, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .,}\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial)}

\NormalTok{tbl.glm }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(grammatical}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{response, }\FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm.C, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"response"}\NormalTok{)}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{colnames}\NormalTok{(tbl.glm) }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grammatical"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ungrammatical"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{tbl.glm}

\subsubsection{GLM: Other distributions}\label{glm-other-distributions}

If your data does not fit a binomial distribution, and is a multinomial
(i.e., three or more response categories) or poisson (count data), then
you need to use the glm function with a specific family function.

\section{Cumulative Logit Link Models}\label{CLM}

These models work perfectly with rating data. Ratings are inherently
ordered, 1, 2, \ldots{} n, and expect to observe an increase (or decrease) in
overall ratings from 1 to n.~To demonstrate this, we will use an example
using the package ``ordinal''.

We use two datasets. We previously ran these two models, however, in
this subset of the full dataset, we did not take into account the fact
that there were multiple producing speakers and items.

\subsection{Ratings of percept of nasality}\label{ratings-of-percept-of-nasality}

The first comes from a likert-scale a rating experiment where six
participants rated the percept of nasality in the production of
particular consonants in Arabic. The data came from nine producing
subjects. The ratings were from 1 to 5, with 1 reflecting an \texttt{oral}
percept; 5 a \texttt{nasal} percept.

\subsubsection{Importing and pre-processing}\label{importing-and-pre-processing}

We start by importing the data and process it. We change the reference
level in the predictor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rating }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{read\_csv}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"data/rating.csv"}\NormalTok{)[}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{rating}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 405 x 5
##    Response Context   Subject Item    Rater
##       <dbl> <chr>     <chr>   <chr>   <chr>
##  1        2 n-3       p04     noo3-w  R01  
##  2        4 isolation p04     noo3-v  R01  
##  3        2 o-3       p04     djuu3-w R01  
##  4        4 isolation p04     djuu3-v R01  
##  5        3 n-7       p04     nuu7-w  R01  
##  6        3 isolation p04     nuu7-v  R01  
##  7        1 3--3      p04     3oo3-w  R01  
##  8        2 isolation p04     3oo3-v  R01  
##  9        2 o-7       p04     loo7-w  R01  
## 10        1 o-3       p04     bii3-w  R01  
## # i 395 more rows
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rating }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ rating }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{Response =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(Response),}
         \AttributeTok{Context =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(Context)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{Context =} \FunctionTok{relevel}\NormalTok{(Context, }\StringTok{"isolation"}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{rating}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 405 x 5
##    Response Context   Subject Item    Rater
##    <fct>    <fct>     <chr>   <chr>   <chr>
##  1 2        n-3       p04     noo3-w  R01  
##  2 4        isolation p04     noo3-v  R01  
##  3 2        o-3       p04     djuu3-w R01  
##  4 4        isolation p04     djuu3-v R01  
##  5 3        n-7       p04     nuu7-w  R01  
##  6 3        isolation p04     nuu7-v  R01  
##  7 1        3--3      p04     3oo3-w  R01  
##  8 2        isolation p04     3oo3-v  R01  
##  9 2        o-7       p04     loo7-w  R01  
## 10 1        o-3       p04     bii3-w  R01  
## # i 395 more rows
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Our first model}\label{our-first-model}

We run our first clm model as a simple, i.e., with no random effects

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.clm }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ rating }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{clm}\NormalTok{(Response }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ Context, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.clm)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Testing significance}\label{testing-significance}

We can evaluate whether ``Context'' improves the model fit, by comparing a
null model with our model. Of course ``Context'' is improving the model
fit.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.clm.Null }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ rating }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{clm}\NormalTok{(Response }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\FunctionTok{anova}\NormalTok{(mdl.clm, mdl.clm.Null)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models:
##  
##              formula:           link: threshold:
## mdl.clm.Null Response ~ 1       logit flexible  
## mdl.clm      Response ~ Context logit flexible  
## 
##              no.par    AIC  logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq)    
## mdl.clm.Null      4 1281.1 -636.56                          
## mdl.clm          17 1086.3 -526.16   220.8 13  < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Model's fit}\label{models-fit-4}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{tab\_model}\NormalTok{(mdl.clm, }\AttributeTok{file =} \FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"outputs/mdl.clm.html"}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{htmltools}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{includeHTML}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"outputs/mdl.clm.html"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}

\subsubsection{Interpreting a cumulative model}\label{interpreting-a-cumulative-model}

As a way to interpret the model, we can look at the coefficients and
make sense of the results. A CLM model is a Logistic model with a
cumulative effect. The ``Coefficients'' are the estimates for each level
of the fixed effect; the ``Threshold coefficients'' are those of the
response. For the former, a negative coefficient indicates a negative
association with the response; and a positive is positively associated
with the response. The p values are indicating the significance of each
level. For the ``Threshold coefficients'', we can see the cumulative
effects of ratings 1\textbar2, 2\textbar3, 3\textbar4 and 4\textbar5 which indicate an overall
increase in the ratings from 1 to 5.

\paragraph{Plotting}\label{plotting-3}
