\section{GLM as a classification tool}\label{glm-as-a-classification-tool}

\subsection{Model specification}\label{model-specification-1}

Let's run a first GLM (Generalised Linear Model). A GLM uses a special family ``binomial'' as it assumes the outcome has a binomial distribution. In general, results from a Logistic Regression are close to what we get from SDT.

We will use the same dataset that comes from phonetic research. This dataset is from my current work on the \texttt{phonetic\ basis\ of\ the\ guttural\ natural\ class\ in\ Levantine\ Arabic}. Acoustic analyses were conducted on multiple portions of the VCV sequence, and we report here the averaged results on the first half of V2. Acoustic metrics were obtained via VoiceSauce: various acoustic metrics of supralaryngeal (bark difference) and laryngeal (voice quality via amplitude harmonic differences, noise, energy) were obtained. A total of 23 different acoustic metrics were obtained from 10 participants. Here, we use the data from the first two participants for demonstration purposes (one male and one female). The grouping factor of interest is context with two levels: \texttt{guttural} vs \texttt{non-guttural}. Gutturals include uvular, pharyngealised and pharyngeal consonants; non-gutturals include coronal plain, velar and glottal consonants.

The aim of the study was to evaluate whether the combination of the acoustic metrics provides support for a difference between the two classes of gutturals vs non-gutturals.

We run a GLM with \texttt{context} as our outcome, and \texttt{Z2-Z1} as our predictor. We want to evaluate whether the two classes can be separated when using the acoustic metric \texttt{Z2-Z1}. Context has two levels, and this will be considered as a binomial distribution.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mdl.glm.Z2mnZ1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ Z2mnZ1, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial)}
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm.Z2mnZ1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = context ~ Z2mnZ1, family = binomial, data = .)
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)  0.50112    0.23036   2.175 0.029605 *  
## Z2mnZ1      -0.12281    0.03621  -3.391 0.000696 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 552.89  on 401  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 541.01  on 400  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 545.01
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm.Z2mnZ1) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(term, estimate) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{estimate =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(estimate, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 2 x 2
##   term        estimate
##   <chr>          <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)    0.501
## 2 Z2mnZ1        -0.123
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\# to only get the coefficients}
\NormalTok{mycoef2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{tidy}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm.Z2mnZ1) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{pull}\NormalTok{(estimate)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Plogis}\label{plogis}

The result above shows that when moving from the \texttt{non-guttural} (intercept), a unit increase (i.e., \texttt{guttural}) yields a statistically significant decrease in the log odds associated with \texttt{Z2-Z1}. We can evaluate this further from a classification point of view, using \texttt{plogis}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\# non{-}guttural}
\FunctionTok{plogis}\NormalTok{(mycoef2[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.622722
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#guttural}
\FunctionTok{plogis}\NormalTok{(mycoef2[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ mycoef2[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] 0.5934644
\end{verbatim}

The \texttt{plogis} function provides the probability of being in the \texttt{guttural} class. The intercept (non-guttural) is 0.5, and the \texttt{guttural} class is 0.41. This means that the model predicts that a unit increase in \texttt{Z2-Z1} yields a decrease of 9\% in the probability of being in the \texttt{guttural} class.
This is a small effect, but it is statistically significant. The model also provides the log odds associated with the predictor. The log odds are the natural logarithm of the odds ratio, which is the ratio of the probability of being in one class over the other.
The log odds are not easy to interpret, but they can be used to evaluate the effect of the predictor on the outcome. The log odds for \texttt{Z2-Z1} is -0.1, which means that a unit increase in \texttt{Z2-Z1} yields a decrease of 10\% in the odds of being in the \texttt{guttural} class. This is a small effect, but it is statistically significant.

This shows that \texttt{Z2-Z1} is able to explain the difference in the \texttt{guttural} class with an accuracy of 59\%. Let's continue with this model further.

\subsection{Model predictions}\label{model-predictions}

As above, we obtain predictions from the model. Because we are using a numeric predictor, we need to assign a threshold for the predict function. The threshold can be thought of as telling the predict function to assign any predictions lower than 50\% to one group, and any higher to another.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pred.glm.Z2mnZ1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(mdl.glm.Z2mnZ1, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"response"}\NormalTok{)}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}\FloatTok{0.5}

\NormalTok{tbl.glm.Z2mnZ1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(pred.glm.Z2mnZ1, dfPharV2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{context)}
\FunctionTok{rownames}\NormalTok{(tbl.glm.Z2mnZ1) }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Non{-}Guttural"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Guttural"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{tbl.glm.Z2mnZ1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}

## pred.glm.Z2mnZ1 Non-Guttural Guttural
##    Non-Guttural          167       75
##    Guttural               55      105
\end{verbatim}

\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

## 1   0.5833333     0.03684905
\end{verbatim}

\end{verbatim}

\NormalTok{roc.glm.Z2mnZ1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ pROC}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{roc}\NormalTok{(dfPharV2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{context, }\FunctionTok{as.numeric}\NormalTok{(pred.glm.Z2mnZ1))}

The model above was able to explain the difference between the two classes with an accuracy of 67.7\%. It has a slightly low specificity (0.583) to detect \texttt{gutturals}, but a sightly high sensitivity (0.752) to reject the \texttt{non-gutturals}. Looking at the confusion matrix, we observe that both groups were relatively accurately identified, but we have relatively large errors (or confusions). The AUC is at 0.6678 which is not too high.

Let's continue with GLM to evaluate it further. We start by running a correlation test to evaluate issues with GLM.

\section{Issues with GLM (and regression analyses in general)}\label{issues-with-glm-and-regression-analyses-in-general}

\subsection{Correlation tests}\label{correlation-tests-2}

Below, we look at two predictors that are correlated with each other: \texttt{Z3-Z2} (F3-F2 in Bark) and \texttt{A2*-A3*} (normalised amplitude differences between harmonics closest to F2 and F3). The results of the correlation test shows the two predictors to negatively correlate with each other at a rate of -0.87.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{cor.test}\NormalTok{(dfPharV2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{Z3mnZ2, dfPharV2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{A2mnA3)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  dfPharV2$Z3mnZ2 and dfPharV2$A2mnA3

## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.8947506 -0.8480066
## sample estimates:
##        cor 
## -0.8733751
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{GLM on correlated data}\label{glm-on-correlated-data}

\subsubsection{Model specifications and issues}\label{model-specifications-and-issues}

Let's run a logistic regression as a classification tool to predict the context as a function of each predictor separately and then combined.

## A2mnA3        -0.091045   0.031870  -2.857  0.00428 **

## Residual deviance: 485.41  on 398  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 493.41

## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
\end{verbatim}

When looking at the three models above, it is clear that the log odd value for \texttt{Z3-Z2} is positive, whereas it is negative for \texttt{A2*-A3*}. When adding the two predictors together, there is clear \textbf{suppression}: the coefficients for both predictors are now negative. The relatively high correlation between the predictors affected the coefficients and changed the direction of the slope; collinearity is harmful for any regression analysis. When we use an interaction term, the coefficients are all negative, leading to confusions in interpreting the results.

\subsubsection{Checking collinearity}\label{checking-collinearity}

To check for collinearity, we can use the \texttt{vif} function from the \texttt{car} package. The \texttt{vif} stands for the ``Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)''. This is a measure of how much the variance of a regression coefficient is increased due to collinearity. A VIF value below 5 indicates that there is low level of collinearity; between 5 and 10, that there a moderate level of collinearity and above 10 indicates potential collinearity issues.

\paragraph{Simple model}\label{simple-model}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ Z3mnZ2 }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ A2mnA3, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{vif}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##   Z3mnZ2   A2mnA3 
## 4.319093 4.319093
\end{verbatim}

The values here are close to 5, which indicates a moderate level of collinearity. This is appropriate , but it is not ideal either.

\paragraph{Interaction model}\label{interaction-model}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ Z3mnZ2 }\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{ A2mnA3, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{vif}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## there are higher-order terms (interactions) in this model
## consider setting type = 'predictor'; see ?vif
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
##        Z3mnZ2        A2mnA3 Z3mnZ2:A2mnA3 
##      7.151205      7.551354     11.244070
\end{verbatim}

When using interaction, the \texttt{vif} values no increase to more than 5 for the individual predictors, and to 11 for the interaction

We use the function \texttt{check\_collinearity()}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ Z3mnZ2 }\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{ A2mnA3, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{check\_collinearity}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Model has interaction terms. VIFs might be inflated.
##   Try to center the variables used for the interaction, or check
##   multicollinearity among predictors of a model without interaction terms.
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
## # Check for Multicollinearity
## 
## Moderate Correlation
## 
##    Term  VIF    VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
##  Z3mnZ2 7.15 [6.00,  8.57]     2.67      0.14     [0.12, 0.17]
##  A2mnA3 7.55 [6.33,  9.06]     2.75      0.13     [0.11, 0.16]
## 
## High Correlation
## 
##           Term   VIF    VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
##  Z3mnZ2:A2mnA3 11.24 [9.37, 13.53]     3.35      0.09     [0.07, 0.11]
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ Z3mnZ2 }\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{ A2mnA3, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{check\_collinearity}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{plot}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Model has interaction terms. VIFs might be inflated.
##   Try to center the variables used for the interaction, or check
##   multicollinearity among predictors of a model without interaction terms.
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}

\NormalTok{dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}

\begin{verbatim}
## The variance-covariance matrix is not positive definite. Returning the
##   nearest positive definite matrix now.
##   This ensures that eigenvalues are all positive real numbers, and

##   all relevant parameters.
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}

\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
## # Check for Multicollinearity
## 
## Low Correlation
## 
##     Term  VIF           VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
##      CPP 1.00 [    1.00,      Inf]     1.00      1.00     [0.00, 1.00]
##   Energy 1.00 [    1.00,      Inf]     1.00      1.00     [0.00, 1.00]

\subsection{Conclusion}\label{conclusion-4}

The more complex your regression model becomes, the higher level of collinearity one can see. This is a known issue in regression analyses, and without applying appropriate approaches, e.g., verifying the collinearity in the data; choosing non-correlated predictors, etc.., the models become inflated and the confidence in the results becomes reduced.

There are various solutions to this issue, such as removing collinear predictors, using PCA to obtain orthogonal dimension (i.e., non-correlated dimensions), etc.. Another solution is to use decision trees and Random Forest. Both are very well known to deal with collinearity and to make sense of multivariate predictors.

\section{Decision Trees}\label{decision-trees}

Decision trees are a statistical tool that uses the combination of predictors to identify patterns in the data and provides classification accuracy for the model.

The decision tree used is based on \texttt{conditional\ inference\ trees} that looks at each predictor and splits the data into multiple nodes (branches) through recursive partitioning in a \texttt{tree-structured\ regression\ model}. Each node is also split into leaves (difference between levels of outcome).

Decision trees via \texttt{ctree} does the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Test global null hypothesis of independence between predictors and outcome.
\item
  Select the predictor with the strongest association with the outcome measured based on a multiplicity adjusted p-values with Bonferroni correction
\item
  Implement a binary split in the selected input variable.
\item
  Recursively repeat steps 1), 2). and 3).
\end{enumerate}

Let's see this in an example using the same dataset. To understand what the decision tree is doing, we will dissect it, by creating one tree with one predictor and move to the next.

\subsection{Individual trees}\label{individual-trees}

\subsubsection{Tree 1}\label{tree-1}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\# from the package party}
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{tree1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ctree}\NormalTok{(}
\NormalTok{    context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ Z2mnZ1, }
    \AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .)}
\FunctionTok{print}\NormalTok{(tree1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-984-1.pdf}}

How to interpret this figure? Let's look at mean values and a plot for this variable. This is the difference between \texttt{F2} and \texttt{F1} using the bark scale. Because gutturals are produced within the pharynx (regardless of where), the predictions is that a high \texttt{F1} and a low \texttt{F2} will be the acoustic correlates related to this constriction location. The closeness between these formants yields a lower \texttt{Z2-Z1}. Hence, the prediction is as follow: the smaller the difference, the more pharyngeal-like constriction these consonants have (all else being equal!). Let's compute the mean/median and plot the difference between the two contexts.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(context) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{mean =} \FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(Z2mnZ1),}
            \AttributeTok{median =} \FunctionTok{median}\NormalTok{(Z2mnZ1), }
            \AttributeTok{count =} \FunctionTok{n}\NormalTok{())}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 2 x 4
##   context       mean median count
##   <fct>        <dbl>  <dbl> <int>
## 1 Non-Guttural  6.30   5.02   222
## 2 Guttural      5.31   3.84   180
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ context, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ Z2mnZ1)) }\SpecialCharTok{+} 
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{()  }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-985-1.pdf}}

The table above reports the mean and median of \texttt{Z2-Z1} for both levels of context and the plots show the difference between the two. We have a total of 180 cases in the \texttt{guttural}, and 222 in the \texttt{non-guttural}.
When considering the conditional inference tree output, various splits were obtained.
The first is any value higher than 9.55 being assigned to the \texttt{non-guttural} class (around 98\% of 75 cases)
Then, with anything lower than 9.55, a second split was obtained. A threshold of 6.78: higher assigned to \texttt{guttural} (around 98\% of 64 cases), lower, were split again with a threshold of 4 Bark. A third split was obtained: values lower of equal to 4 Bark are assigned to the \texttt{guttural} (around 70\% of 157 cases) and values higher than 4 Barks assigned to the \texttt{non-guttural} (around 90\% of 106 cases).

Dissecting the tree like this allows interpretation of the output. In this example, this is quite a complex case and \texttt{ctree} allowed to fine tune the different patterns seen with
Now let's look at the full dataset to make sense of the combination of predictors to the difference.

We started with \texttt{context} as our outcome, and all 23 acoustic measures as predictors. A total of 8 terminal nodes were identified with multiple binary splits in their leaves, allowing separation of the two categories. Looking specifically at the output, we observe a few things.

The first node was based on \texttt{A2*-A3*}, detecting a difference between non-gutturals and gutturals. For the first binary split, a threshold of -13.78 Bark was used (mean non guttural = -7.86; mean guttural = -14.58), then for values lower of equal to this threshold, a second split was performed using \texttt{Z4-Z3} (mean non guttural = 1.67; mean guttural = 1.43) with any value smaller and equal to 1.59, then another binary split using \texttt{H2*-H4*}, etc\ldots.

Once done, the \texttt{ctree} provides multiple binary splits into guttural or non-guttural.

Any possible issues/interesting patterns you can identify? Look at the interactions between predictors.

This is a good model, but it is not perfect. The confusion matrix shows that the model was able to detect 80\% of the gutturals, but 20\% were misclassified as non-gutturals. The opposite is true for the non-gutturals: 80\% were detected, but 20\% were misclassified as gutturals.
The AUC is at 0.823, which is not too bad.
\#\#\# Random selection

One important issue is that the trees we grew above are biased. They are based on the full dataset, which means they are very likely to overfit the data. We did not add any random selection and we only grew one tree each time. If you think about it, is it possible that we obtained such results simply by chance?

What if we add some randomness in the process of creating a conditional inference tree?

We change a small option in \texttt{ctree} to allow for random selection of variables, to mimic what Random Forests will do. We use \texttt{controls} to specify \texttt{mtry\ =\ 5}, which is the rounded square root of number of predictors.

\subsubsection{Model 2}\label{model-2}

\begin{Shaded}

\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{fit1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2  }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ctree}\NormalTok{(}
\NormalTok{    context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }
    \AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ .,}
    \AttributeTok{controls =} \FunctionTok{ctree\_control}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{mtry =} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{))}

\FunctionTok{plot}\NormalTok{(fit1, }\AttributeTok{main =} \StringTok{"Conditional Inference Tree"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Can you compare results between you and discuss what is going on?

When adding one random selection process to our \texttt{ctree}, we allow it to obtain more robust predictions. We could even go further and grow multiple small trees with a portion of datapoints (e.g., 100 rows, 200 rows). When doing these multiple random selections, you are growing multiple trees that are decorrelated from each other. These become independent trees and one can combine the results of these trees to come with clear predictions.

This is how Random Forests work. You would start from a dataset, then grow multiple trees, vary number of observations used (nrow), and number of predictors used (mtry), adjust branches, and depth of nodes and at the end, combine the results in a forest. You can also run permutation tests to evaluate contributions of each predictor to the outcome. This is the beauty of Random Forests. They do all of these steps automatically at once for you!

\section{Random Forests}\label{random-forests}

As their name indicate, a Random Forest is a forest of trees implemented through bagging ensemble algorithms. Each tree has multiple branches (nodes), and will provide predictions based on recursive partitioning of the data. Then using the predictions from the multiple grown trees, Random Forests will create \texttt{averaged} predictions and come up with prediction accuracy, etc.

There are multiple packages that one can use to grow Random Forests:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{randomForest}: The original implementation of Random Forests.
\item
  \texttt{party} and \texttt{partykit}: using conditional inference trees as base learners
\item
  \texttt{ranger}: a reimplementation of Random Forests; faster and more flexible than original implementation
\end{enumerate}

The first implementation of Random Forests is widely used in research. One of the issues in this first implementation is that it favoured specific types of predictors (e.g., categorical predictors, predictors with multiple cut-offs, etc.). Random Forests grown via Conditional Inference Trees as implemented in \texttt{party} guard against this bias, but they are computationally demanding. Random Forests grown via permutation tests as implemented in \texttt{ranger} speed up the computations and can mimic the unbiased selection process.

\subsection{Party}\label{party}

Random Forests grown via conditional inference trees, are different from the original implementation. They offer an unbiased selection process that guards against overfitting of the data. There are various points we need to consider in growing the forest, including number of trees and predictors to use each time. Let us run our first Random Forest via conditional inference trees. To make sure the code runs as fast as it can, we use a very low number of trees: only 100 It is well known that the more trees you grow, the more confidence you have in the results, as model estimation will be more stable. In this example, I would easily go with 500 trees..

\subsubsection{Model specification}\label{model-specification-3}

To grow the forest, we use the function \texttt{cforest}. We use all of the dataset for the moment. We need to specify a few options within controls:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{ntree\ =\ 100} = number of trees to grow. Default = 500.
\item
  \texttt{mtry\ =\ round(sqrt(23))}: number of predictors to use each time. Default is 5, but specifying it is advised to account for the structure of the data
\end{enumerate}

By default, \texttt{cforest\_unbiased} has two additional important options that are used for an unbiased selection process. \textbf{WARNING}: you should not change these unless you know what you are doing. Also, by default, the data are split into a training and a testing set. The training is equal to 2/3s of the data; the testing is 1/3.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{replace\ =\ FALSE} = Use subsampling with or without replacement. Default is \texttt{FALSE}, i.e., use subsets of the data without replacing these.\\
\item
  \texttt{fraction\ =\ 0.632} = Use 63.2\% of the data in each split.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{mdl.cforest }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{cforest}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }
          \AttributeTok{controls =} \FunctionTok{cforest\_unbiased}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{ntree =} \DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{, }
                                      \AttributeTok{mtry =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{sqrt}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{23}\NormalTok{))))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Predictions}\label{predictions}

To obtain predictions from the model, we use the \texttt{predict} function and add \texttt{OOB\ =\ TRUE}. This uses the out-of-bag sample (i.e., 1/3 of the data).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{pred.cforest }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(mdl.cforest, }\AttributeTok{OOB =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{tbl.cforest }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(pred.cforest, dfPharV2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{context)}
\NormalTok{tbl.cforest}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-991-1.pdf}}

Compared with the 82.8\% classification accuracy we obtained using \texttt{ctree} using our full dataset above (model 1), here we obtain 84.8\%; a 2\% increase in classification accuracy. The specificity is slightly lower at 0.761 (at detecting the gutturals), but the sensitivity is higher at 0.919 (at detecting the non-gutturals). The ROC curve shows the relationship between the two with an AUC of 0.84.

We could test whether there is statistically significant difference between our \texttt{ctree} and \texttt{cforest} models. Using the ROC curves, the \texttt{roc.test} conducts a non-parametric Z test of significance on the correlated ROC curves. The results show a statistically significant improvement using the \texttt{cforest} model. This is normal because we are growing 100 different trees, with random selection of both predictors and samples and provide an \texttt{averaged} prediction.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pROC}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{roc.test}\NormalTok{(roc.ctree, roc.cforest)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  DeLong's test for two correlated ROC curves
## 
## data:  roc.ctree and roc.cforest
## Z = -0.7417, p-value = 0.4583
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in AUC is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.06180273  0.02786879
## sample estimates:
## AUC of roc1 AUC of roc2 
##    0.823048    0.840015
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pROC}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{roc.test}\NormalTok{(roc.ctree1, roc.cforest)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
##  DeLong's test for two correlated ROC curves
## 
## data:  roc.ctree1 and roc.cforest
## Z = -4.2372, p-value = 2.264e-05
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in AUC is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.14296247 -0.05253302
## sample estimates:
## AUC of roc1 AUC of roc2 
##   0.7422673   0.8400150
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Variable Importance Scores}\label{variable-importance-scores}

One important feature in \texttt{ctree} was to show which predictor was used first is splitting the data, which was then followed by the other predictors. We use a similar functionality with \texttt{cforest} to obtain variable importance scores to pinpoint \texttt{strong} and \texttt{weak} predictors.

There are two ways to obtain this:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Simple permutation tests (conditional = FALSE)
\item
  Conditional permutation tests (conditional = TRUE)
\end{enumerate}

The former is generally comparable across packages and provides a normal permutation test; the latter runs a permutation test on a grid defined by the correlation matrix and corrects for possible collinearity. This is similar to a regression analysis, but looks at both main effects and interactions.

You could use the normal \texttt{varimp} as implemented in \texttt{party}. This uses mean decrease in accuracy scores. We will use variable importance scores via an AUC based permutation tests as this uses both accuracy and errors in the model, using \texttt{varImpAUC} from the \texttt{varImp} package.

\textbf{DANGER ZONE}: using conditional permutation test requires a lot of RAMs, unless you have access to a cluster, and/or a lot of RAMs, do not attempt running it. We will run the non-conditional version here for demonstration.

\paragraph{Non-conditional permutation tests}\label{non-conditional-permutation-tests}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{VarImp.cforest }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ varImp}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{varImpAUC}\NormalTok{(mdl.cforest, }\AttributeTok{conditional =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{lattice}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{barchart}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{sort}\NormalTok{(VarImp.cforest))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-993-1.pdf}}

The Variable Importance Scores via non-conditional permutation tests showed that \texttt{A2*-A3*} (i.e., energy in mid-high frequencies around F2 and F3) is the most important variable at explaining the difference between gutturals and non-gutturals, followed by \texttt{Z4-Z3} (pharyngeal constriction), \texttt{H1*-A3*} (energy in mid-high frequency component), \texttt{Z2-Z1} (degree of compactness), \texttt{Z3-Z2} (spectral divergence), \texttt{H1*-A2} (energy in mid frequency component) and \texttt{Z1-Z0} (degree of openness). All other predictors contribute to the contrast but to varying degrees (from \texttt{H1*-H2*} to \texttt{H1*-A1*}). The last 5 predictors are the least important and and the CPP has a 0 mean decrease in accuracy and can even be ignored.

\paragraph{Conditional permutation tests}\label{conditional-permutation-tests}

On this relatively small dataset, the conditional permutation tests were relatively fast. Be careful with larger datasets.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{VarImp.cforest }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ varImp}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{varImpAUC}\NormalTok{(mdl.cforest, }\AttributeTok{conditional =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{lattice}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{barchart}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{sort}\NormalTok{(VarImp.cforest))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-994-1.pdf}}

\subsubsection{Conclusion}\label{conclusion-5}

The \texttt{party} package is powerful at growing Random Forests via conditional Inference trees, but is computationally prohibitive when increasing number of trees and using conditional permutation tests of variable importance scores. We look next at the package \texttt{ranger} due to its speed in computation and flexibility.

\subsection{Ranger}\label{ranger}

\subsubsection{Declare parallel computing}\label{declare-parallel-computing}

We start by declaring parallel computing on your devices. This is essential to run these complex computations. The code below is designed to only use 1 core from your machine (and it is not too complex), but if you try to increase the complexity of your computations, you will need parallel computing.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\#Declare parallel computing }
\NormalTok{ncores }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{availableCores}\NormalTok{()}
\FunctionTok{cat}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Number of cores available for model calculations set to "}\NormalTok{, ncores, }\StringTok{"."}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Number of cores available for model calculations set to 12.
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{registerDoFuture}\NormalTok{()}
\FunctionTok{makeClusterPSOCK}\NormalTok{(ncores)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Socket cluster with 12 nodes on host 'localhost' (R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31 ucrt), platform x86_64-w64-mingw32)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{plan}\NormalTok{(multisession)}
\NormalTok{ncores}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## system 
##     12
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\# below we register our random number generator. This will mostly be used within the tidymodels below. This allows replication of the results}
\DocumentationTok{\#\# below to suppress any warnings from doFuture}
\FunctionTok{options}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{doFuture.rng.onMisuse =} \StringTok{"ignore"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The \texttt{ranger} package proposes a reimplementation of the original Random Forests algorithms, written in C++ and allows for parallel computing. It offers more flexibility in terms of model specification.

\subsubsection{Model specification}\label{model-specification-4}

In the model below specification below, there are already a few options we are familiar with, with additional ones described below:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{num.tree} = Number of trees to grow. We use the default value
\item
  \texttt{mtry} = Number of predictors to use. Default = \texttt{floor(sqrt(Variables))}. For compatibility with \texttt{party}, we use \texttt{round(sqrt(23))}
\item
  \texttt{replace\ =\ FALSE} = Use subsampling with or without replacement. Default \texttt{replace\ =\ TRUE}, i.e., is \textbf{with} replacement.
\item
  \texttt{sample.fraction\ =\ 0.632} = Use 63.2\% of the data in each split. Default is full dataset, i.e., \texttt{sample.fraction\ =\ 1}
\item
  \texttt{importance\ =\ "permutation"} = Compute variable importance scores via permutation tests
\item
  \texttt{scale.permutation.importance\ =\ FALSE} = whether to scale variable importance scores to be out of 100\%. Default is TRUE. This is likely to introduce biases in variable importance estimation.
\item
  \texttt{splitrule\ =\ "extratrees"} = rule used for splitting trees.
\item
  \texttt{num.threads} = allow for parallel computing. Here we only specify 1 thread, but can use all thread on your computer (or cluster).
\end{enumerate}

We use options 2-7 to make sure we have an unbiased selection process with \texttt{ranger}. You can try on your own running the model below by using the defaults to see how the rate of classification increases more, but with the caveat that it has a biased selection process.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{mdl.ranger }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ranger}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{num.trees =} \DecValTok{500}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{mtry =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{sqrt}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{23}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sample.fraction =} \FloatTok{0.632}\NormalTok{, }
         \AttributeTok{importance =} \StringTok{"permutation"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{scale.permutation.importance =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{,}
         \AttributeTok{splitrule =} \StringTok{"extratrees"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{num.threads =}\NormalTok{ ncores)}
\NormalTok{mdl.ranger}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Ranger result
## 
## Call:
##  ranger(context ~ ., data = ., num.trees = 500, mtry = round(sqrt(23)),      replace = FALSE, sample.fraction = 0.632, importance = "permutation",      scale.permutation.importance = FALSE, splitrule = "extratrees",      num.threads = ncores) 
## 
## Type:                             Classification 
## Number of trees:                  500 
## Sample size:                      402 
## Number of independent variables:  23 
## Mtry:                             5 
## Target node size:                 1 
## Variable importance mode:         permutation 
## Splitrule:                        extratrees 
## Number of random splits:          1 
## OOB prediction error:             7.46 %
\end{verbatim}

Results of our Random Forest shows an OOB (Out-Of-Bag) error rate of 7.46\%, i.e., an accuracy of 92.54\%.

\subsubsection{Going further}\label{going-further}

Unfortunately, when growing a tree with \texttt{ranger}, we cannot use predictions from the OOB sample as there are no comparable options to do so on the predictions. We need to hard-code this. We split the data into a training and a testing sets. The training will be on 2/3s of the data; the testing is on the remaining 1/3.

\paragraph{Create a training and a testing set}\label{create-a-training-and-a-testing-set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{train.idx }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(dfPharV2), }\DecValTok{2}\SpecialCharTok{/}\DecValTok{3} \SpecialCharTok{*} \FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(dfPharV2))}
\NormalTok{gutt.train }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2[train.idx, ]}
\NormalTok{gutt.test }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2[}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{train.idx, ]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{Model specification}\label{model-specification-5}

We use the same model specification as above, except from using the training set and saving the forest (with \texttt{write.forest\ =\ TRUE}).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{mdl.ranger2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ gutt.train }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{ranger}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{num.trees =} \DecValTok{500}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{mtry =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{sqrt}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{23}\NormalTok{)),}
         \AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sample.fraction =} \FloatTok{0.632}\NormalTok{, }
         \AttributeTok{importance =} \StringTok{"permutation"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{scale.permutation.importance =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{,}
         \AttributeTok{splitrule =} \StringTok{"extratrees"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{num.threads =}\NormalTok{ ncores, }\AttributeTok{write.forest =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{mdl.ranger2}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## Ranger result
## 
## Call:
##  ranger(context ~ ., data = ., num.trees = 500, mtry = round(sqrt(23)),      replace = FALSE, sample.fraction = 0.632, importance = "permutation",      scale.permutation.importance = FALSE, splitrule = "extratrees",      num.threads = ncores, write.forest = TRUE) 
## 
## Type:                             Classification 
## Number of trees:                  500 
## Sample size:                      268 
## Number of independent variables:  23 
## Mtry:                             5 
## Target node size:                 1 
## Variable importance mode:         permutation 
## Splitrule:                        extratrees 
## Number of random splits:          1 
## OOB prediction error:             10.82 %
\end{verbatim}

With the training set, we have an OOB error rate of 10.82\%; i.e., an accuracy rate of 89.18\%.

\paragraph{Predictions}\label{predictions-1}

For the predictions, we use the testing set as a validation set. This is to be considered as a true reflection of the model. This is unseen data not used in the training set.

\begin{Shaded}

\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{pred.ranger2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(mdl.ranger2, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ gutt.test)}
\NormalTok{tbl.ranger2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(pred.ranger2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{predictions, gutt.test}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{context)}
\NormalTok{tbl.ranger2}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The classification rate based on the testing set is 91.1\%. This is comparable to the one we obtained with \texttt{cforest}. The changes in the settings allow for similarities in the predictions obtained from both \texttt{party} and \texttt{ranger}.

\paragraph{Variable Importance Scores}\label{variable-importance-scores-1}

\subparagraph{Default}\label{default-1}

For the variable importance scores, we obtain them from either the training set or the full model above.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{lattice}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{barchart}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{sort}\NormalTok{(mdl.ranger2}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{variable.importance), }\AttributeTok{main =} \StringTok{"Variable Importance scores {-} training set"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-1000-1.pdf}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{lattice}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{barchart}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{sort}\NormalTok{(mdl.ranger}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{variable.importance), }\AttributeTok{main =} \StringTok{"Variable Importance scores {-} full set"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Statistics-for-Linguists-using-R_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-1000-2.pdf}}

There are similarities between \texttt{cforest} and \texttt{ranger}, with minor differences. \texttt{Z2-Z1} is the best predictor at explaining the differences between gutturals and non-gutturals with \texttt{ranger} followed by \texttt{Z3-Z2} and then \texttt{A2*-A3*}, (reverse with \texttt{cforest}!). The order of the additional predictors is sightly different between the two models. This is expected as the \texttt{cforest} model only used 100 trees, whereas the \texttt{ranger} model used 500 trees.

A clear difference between the packages \texttt{party} and \texttt{ranger} is that the former allows for conditional permutation tests for variable importance scores; this is absent from \texttt{ranger}. However, there is a debate in the literature on whether correlated data are harmful within Random Forests. It is clear that how Random Forests work, i.e., the randomness in the selection process in number of data points, predictors, splitting rules, etc. allow the trees to be decorrelated from each other. Hence, the conditional permutation tests may not be required. But what they offer is to condition variable importance scores on each other (based on correlation tests) to mimic what a multiple regression analysis does (but without suffering from suppression!). Strong predictors will show major contribution, while weak ones will be squashed giving them extremely low (or even negative) scores. Within \texttt{ranger}, it is possible to evaluate this by estimating p values associated with each variable importance.We use the \texttt{altman} method. See documentation for more details.

\textbf{DANGER ZONE}: This requires heavy computations. Use with all cores on your machine or in the cluster. Recommendations are to use a minimum of 500 permutations or more, i.e., \texttt{num.permutations\ =\ 500}; ideally 1000 or more permutations are needed to get an accurate picture\ldots{}

\subparagraph{With p values}\label{with-p-values}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{VarImp.pval }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{importance\_pvalues}\NormalTok{(mdl.ranger2, }\AttributeTok{method =} \StringTok{"altmann"}\NormalTok{,}
                                  \AttributeTok{num.permutations =} \DecValTok{2000}\NormalTok{, }
                                  \AttributeTok{formula =}\NormalTok{ context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ gutt.train,}
                                  \AttributeTok{num.threads =}\NormalTok{ ncores)}
\NormalTok{VarImp.pvaldf }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ VarImp.pval }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{as.data.frame}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{rownames\_to\_column}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{var =} \StringTok{"correlate"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{arrange}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{desc}\NormalTok{(importance))}
\NormalTok{VarImp.pvaldf}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Of course, the output above shows variable p values. The lowest is at 0.0004997501 for all predictors; one at 0.0364817591 for CPP. Recall that CPP received the lowest variable importance score within \texttt{ranger} and \texttt{cforest}.

In the next part, we look at the \texttt{tidymodels} and introduce their philosophy.

\subsection{Random forests with Tidymodels}\label{random-forests-with-tidymodels}

The \texttt{tidymodels} are a bundle of packages used to streamline and simplify the use of machine learning. The \texttt{tidymodels} are not restricted to Random Forests, and you can even use them to run simple linear models, logistic regressions, PCA, Random Forests, Deep Learning, etc.

The \texttt{tidymodels}' philosophy is to separate data processing on the training and testing sets, and use of a workflow. Below, is an full example of how one can run Random Forests with via \texttt{ranger} using the \texttt{tidymodels}.

\subsubsection{Training and testing sets}\label{training-and-testing-sets}

We start by creating a training and a testing set using the function \texttt{initial\_split}. Using \texttt{strata\ =\ context} allows the model to split the data taking into account its structure and splits the data according to proportions of each group.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{train\_test\_split }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}
  \FunctionTok{initial\_split}\NormalTok{(}
    \AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ dfPharV2,}
    \AttributeTok{strata =} \StringTok{"context"}\NormalTok{,}
    \AttributeTok{prop =} \FloatTok{0.667}\NormalTok{) }
\NormalTok{train\_test\_split}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## <Training/Testing/Total>
## <268/134/402>
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{train\_tbl }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ train\_test\_split }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{training}\NormalTok{() }
\NormalTok{test\_tbl  }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ train\_test\_split }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{testing}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Set for cross-validation}\label{set-for-cross-validation}

We can (if we want to), create a 10-folds cross-validation on the training set. This allows to fine tune the training by obtaining the forest with the highest accuracy. This is a clear difference with \texttt{ranger}. While it is not impossible to hard code that, \texttt{tidymodels} simplify it for us!!

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{train\_cv }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{vfold\_cv}\NormalTok{(train\_tbl, }\AttributeTok{v =} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{strata =} \StringTok{"context"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Model Specification}\label{model-specification-6}

Within the model specification, we need to specify multiple options:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A \texttt{recipe}: This is the recipe and is related to any data processing one wants to apply on the data.
\item
  An \texttt{engine}: We need to specify the \texttt{engine} to use. Here we want to run a Random Forest.
\item
  A \texttt{tuning}: Here we can tune our engine
\item
  A \texttt{workflow}: here we specify the various steps of the workflow
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Recipe}\label{recipe}

When defining the recipe, you need to think of the type of ``transformations'' you will apply to your data.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Z-scoring is the first thing that comes to mind. When you z-score the data, you are allowing all strong and weak predictors to be considered equally by the model. This is important as some of our predictors have very large differences related to the levels of context and have different measurement scales. We could have applied it above, but we need to make sure to apply it separately on both training and testing sets (otherwise, our model suffers from data leakage)
\item
  If you have any missing data, you can use central imputations to fill in missing data (random forests do not like missing data, though they can work with them).
\item
  You can apply PCA on all your predictors to remove collinearity before running random forests. This is a great option to consider, but adds more complexity to your model.
  4.Finally, if you have categorical predictors, you can transform them into dummy variables using \texttt{step\_dummy()}: 1s and 2s for binary; or use one-hot-encoding \texttt{step\_dummy(predictor,\ one\_hot\ =\ TRUE)}
\end{enumerate}

See documentations of \texttt{tidymodels} for what you can apply!!

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{recipe }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}  
\NormalTok{  train\_tbl }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{recipe}\NormalTok{(context }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ .) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{step\_center}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{all\_predictors}\NormalTok{(), }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\FunctionTok{all\_outcomes}\NormalTok{()) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{step\_scale}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{all\_predictors}\NormalTok{(), }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\FunctionTok{all\_outcomes}\NormalTok{())}

\NormalTok{recipePrep }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ recipe }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{prep}\NormalTok{()}

\NormalTok{trainData\_baked }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{bake}\NormalTok{(recipePrep, }\AttributeTok{new\_data =}\NormalTok{ train\_tbl) }\DocumentationTok{\#\# convert to the train data to the newly imputed data}

\NormalTok{trainData\_prep }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ recipe }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{prep}\NormalTok{()}

\NormalTok{trainData\_baked }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{bake}\NormalTok{(trainData\_prep, }\AttributeTok{new\_data =}\NormalTok{ train\_tbl) }\DocumentationTok{\#\# convert to the train data to the newly imputed data}
\NormalTok{trainData\_baked}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 268 x 24

## 10 -1.06   2.63  -0.266   0.147   1.78  -0.682 -0.336   -1.40     1.06   -0.972
## # i 258 more rows

## #   F0Bark <dbl>, A1mnA2 <dbl>, A1mnA3 <dbl>, A2mnA3 <dbl>, context <fct>
\end{verbatim}

Once we have prepared the \texttt{recipe}, we can \texttt{bake\ it} to see the changes applied to it.

\paragraph{Setting the engine}\label{setting-the-engine}

We set the engine here as a \texttt{rand\_forest}. We specify a classification mode. Then, we set an engine with engine specific parameters.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{engine\_tidym }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{rand\_forest}\NormalTok{(}
    \AttributeTok{mode =} \StringTok{"classification"}\NormalTok{,}
    \AttributeTok{engine =} \StringTok{"ranger"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{    mtry }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{tune}\NormalTok{(),}
\NormalTok{    trees }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{tune}\NormalTok{(),}
    \AttributeTok{min\_n =} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{  ) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{set\_engine}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"ranger"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{importance =} \StringTok{"permutation"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sample.fraction =} \FloatTok{0.632}\NormalTok{,}
             \AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{write.forest =}\NormalTok{ T, }\AttributeTok{splitrule =} \StringTok{"extratrees"}\NormalTok{,}
             \AttributeTok{scale.permutation.importance =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{) }\DocumentationTok{\#\# we add engine specific settings}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{Settings for tuning}\label{settings-for-tuning}

If we want to tune the model, then uncomment the lines below. It is important to use an mtry that hovers around the round(sqrt(Variables)). If you use all available variables, then your forest is biased as it is able to see all predictors. For number of trees, low numbers are not great, as you can easily underfit the data and not produce meaningful results. Large numbers are fine and Random Forests do not overfit (in theory).

The full dataset has around 2000 observations, and 23 predictors (well even more, but let's ignore it for the moment). I tuned \texttt{mtry} to be between 4 and 6, and \texttt{trees} to be between 1000 and 5000 in a 30 step increment. In total, with a 10-folds cross validation, I grew 30 random forests on each fold for a total of 300 Random Forests on the training set!!! This of course will take a loooooong time to compute on your computer if using one thread. So use parallel computing or a cluster. When running in the cluster with 20 cores, each with 11GB RAMs, and it took around 260.442 seconds to run with 220GB RAMS! Of course, with smaller RAMs and number of cores, the code will still run but will take longer.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{gridy\_tidym }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{grid\_random}\NormalTok{(}
  \FunctionTok{mtry}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{range\_set}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)),}
  \FunctionTok{trees}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{range\_set}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2000}\NormalTok{)),}
  \AttributeTok{size =} \DecValTok{30}
\NormalTok{  )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{Workflow}\label{workflow}

Now we define the workflow adding the \texttt{recipe} and the \texttt{model}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{wkfl\_tidym }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{workflow}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{add\_recipe}\NormalTok{(recipe) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{add\_model}\NormalTok{(engine\_tidym)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{Tuning and running model}\label{tuning-and-running-model}

Here we run the model starting with the workflow, the cross-validation sample, the tuning parameters and asking for specific metrics.

The model below will do the following:
1. Use a 10-folds cross validation on the training test
2. Tune the hyper-parameters to reach the model with the best predictions
3. Within each fold, we grow 30 random forests; we have a total of 300 Random Forests, and we use an ROC-AUC based search for the best performing model

Of course, you could use a larger size to grow more trees, with this will take longer to run!

The model will run for about 2-3 minutes with an 8 cores machine and 32GB of RAMs. For demonstration purposes, the tuning of number of trees is restricted to between 1000 and 2000 trees. This can of course be increased to 5000 trees (or more) depending on the size of the dataset

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{system.time}\NormalTok{(grid\_tidym }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} 
  \FunctionTok{tune\_grid}\NormalTok{(wkfl\_tidym, }
            \AttributeTok{resamples =}\NormalTok{ train\_cv,}
            \AttributeTok{grid =}\NormalTok{ gridy\_tidym,}
            \AttributeTok{metrics =} \FunctionTok{metric\_set}\NormalTok{(accuracy, roc\_auc, sens, spec,f\_meas, precision, recall),}
            \AttributeTok{control =} \FunctionTok{control\_grid}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{save\_pred =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{parallel\_over =} \ConstantTok{NULL}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##    user  system elapsed 
##    0.98    0.28   63.32
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{print}\NormalTok{(grid\_tidym)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\FunctionTok{collect\_metrics}\NormalTok{(grid\_tidym)}

\paragraph{Gains curves}\label{gains-curves}

This is an interesting features that show how much is gained when looking at various portions of the data. We see a gradual increase in the values. When 50\% of the data were tested, around 83\% of the results within the non-guttural class were already identified. The more testing was performed, the more confidence in the results there are and then when 84.96\% of the data were tested, 100\% of the cases were found.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{wkfl\_tidym\_final}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{.predictions[[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]] }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{gain\_curve}\NormalTok{(context, }\StringTok{\textasciigrave{}}\AttributeTok{.pred\_Non{-}Guttural}\StringTok{\textasciigrave{}}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{autoplot}\NormalTok{() }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is the end of this chapter introducing Random Forests. We have seen how to run them using \texttt{party}, \texttt{ranger} and \texttt{tidymodels}. The latter is a great package that allows to streamline the process of running machine learning models. It is not restricted to Random Forests, and can be used for any type of model!
